### New Feature for Release

PyTorch 2.15 brings several enhancements to the Intel XPU, including simplified kernel programming, expanded runtime capabilities, and improved profiling support.

### Point(s) of contact

riverliuintel; EikanWang

### Release Mode (pytorch/pytorch features only)

In-tree

### Out-Of-Tree Repo

_No response_

### Description and value to the user

**SYCL Kernel Programming Simplified**
This release introduces SYCL free-function kernel support for the XPU backend, with most existing SYCL kernels already migrated to the new programming model. By replacing verbose functor-based implementations with explicit free-function kernels, developers can write device code in a more intuitive, significantly lowering the barrier to developing and porting custom GPU kernels for Intel XPUs. (PR #[196387](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196387), #[196932](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196932), #[198200](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198200), #[198720](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198720), and #[200223](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200223) by Intel)
**Enhanced XPU Runtime Capabilities** 
This release expands XPU runtime capabilities with IPC support for torch.xpu.Event, enabling event sharing across processes and seamless integration with torch.multiprocessing. In addition, torch.xpu.MemPool now supports use_on_oom and non_split allocation policies, providing greater flexibility for applications that need to handle out-of-memory conditions or leverage distributed symmetric-memory workflows. (PR [#191182](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/191182),  [#192495](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192495), [#192514](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192514), [#192038](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192038) and [#192033](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192033) by Guangye Yu, Intel )
**Improved XPU Profiling Experience**
This release adds kernel-level visibility into XPU Graph replay, cross-rank correlation for XCCL collectives, and per-kernel hardware counter collection across all Intel GPUs in multi-GPU workloads. These enhancements enable deeper performance analysis for graph-based, multi-GPU, and distributed training and inference. (PR [#195128](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/195128/) by Chuanqi Wang, Intel; PR [torch-xpu-ops #5486](https://github.com/intel/torch-xpu-ops/pull/5486) and [Kineto #1479](https://github.com/pytorch/kineto/pull/1479) by Adrian Ostrowski, Intel)

_No response_

N/A

Tutorial exists

https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/notes/get_start_xpu.html

### Marketing/Blog Coverage

Yes

N/A

PyTorch 2.15

### OS / Platform / Compute Coverage

Linux and Windows, Intel GPUs

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On MPS, fp32 convolutions with at least 16 input and 16 output channels return wrong values, with no error or warning, once the batch dimension reaches 2^16:

- `conv2d` and `conv_transpose1d`: every sample at batch index ≥ 65536 is wrong; samples 0..65535 are correct.
- `conv_transpose2d`: at batch ≥ 65536, the **last** 65536 samples are wrong (at batch 65536 that is every sample; at batch 100000 it is rows 34464..99999). Batch 65535 is correct.
- `conv1d` had the same bug in 2.10.0 and 2.11.0 and is **fixed in nightly 2.16.0.dev20261014**. The other three are still broken in that nightly.

Errors are of the order of the outputs themselves, not rounding. They do not depend on spatial size or sequence length. They do not occur with ≤ 8 input or output channels, in fp16, in bf16, in conv3d, in conv1d's backward pass, or in linear/bmm with > 65536 rows.

Minimal repro:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
print(torch.__version__)
cases = {
    "conv1d": (F.conv1d, (32, 16), (32, 32, 1)),
    "conv2d": (F.conv2d, (32, 4, 4), (32, 32, 1, 1)),
    "conv_transpose1d": (F.conv_transpose1d, (32, 16), (32, 32, 3)),
    "conv_transpose2d": (F.conv_transpose2d, (32, 4, 4), (32, 32, 3, 3)),
}
for name, (op, in_shape, w_shape) in cases.items():
    w = torch.randn(w_shape)
    for n in (65536, 65537, 100000):
        x = torch.randn(n, *in_shape)
        ref = op(x, w)
        out = op(x.to("mps"), w.to("mps")).cpu()
        bad = ((out - ref).abs().flatten(1).amax(1) > 1e-2).nonzero().flatten()
        detail = f", rows {bad.min().item()}..{bad.max().item()}" if len(bad) else ""
        print(f"{name:17s} batch={n:6d}: {len(bad):5d} wrong rows{detail}")
```

Output on 2.16.0.dev20261014:

```
conv1d            batch= 65536:     0 wrong rows
conv1d            batch= 65537:     0 wrong rows
conv1d            batch=100000:     0 wrong rows
conv2d            batch= 65536:     0 wrong rows
conv2d            batch= 65537:     1 wrong rows, rows 65536..65536
conv2d            batch=100000: 34464 wrong rows, rows 65536..99999
conv_transpose1d  batch= 65536:     0 wrong rows
conv_transpose1d  batch= 65537:     1 wrong rows, rows 65536..65536
conv_transpose1d  batch=100000: 34464 wrong rows, rows 65536..99999
conv_transpose2d  batch= 65536: 65536 wrong rows, rows 0..65535
conv_transpose2d  batch= 65537: 65536 wrong rows, rows 1..65536
conv_transpose2d  batch=100000: 65536 wrong rows, rows 34464..99999
```

On 2.11.0 the output is identical, except that conv1d also shows 1 and 34464 wrong rows from index 65536. 2.10.0 matches 2.11.0.

The 2^16 cutoff suggests a 16-bit limit on a grid or threadgroup dimension in the fp32 convolution path. Since conv1d was fixed between 2.11 and nightly, the same fix may extend to the other three ops.

How it was found: a small CNN evaluated in one large batch scored 0.63 accuracy on MPS and 0.92 on CPU. Splitting the batch into chunks of at most 65536 samples is a workaround.

Related, but a different trigger: #188335 (grouped Conv2d fp32 wrong at batch > 1, closed).

### Versions

- torch 2.11.0 and 2.10.0 (affected: all four ops); 2.16.0.dev20261014 (affected: conv2d, conv_transpose1d, conv_transpose2d)
- macOS 26.6.1 (25G76), Apple M5 Max
- Python 3.14.3 (2.11.0 and nightly), 3.12.13 (2.10.0)

## Summary

`rerun-disabled-tests` (`PYTORCH_TEST_RERUN_DISABLED_TESTS=1`) reruns tests that are still skipped by a DISABLED GitHub issue, so a run of greens can justify closing that issue. This RFC adds the same kind of signal for a code skip: a skip for a known failure on a machine that can run the test. A capability skip stays skipped. That is a missing library, `onlyCUDA`, `skipIf` / `skipUnless`, `requires_*`, or a version floor.

Two drafts start this work:

- PyTorch, which publishes the signal and does not delete decorators: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra, which would later open one daily draft proposing deletions and does not merge them: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026

## Motivation

| Who | Need |
| --- | --- |
| Test authors | A skip for a known failure can outlive the failure. With no GitHub issue to close, nothing prompts deleting the decorator. |
| CI | The nightly job already reruns DISABLED-issue skips. A code skip never produces a pass or a fail. |

## Background

A DISABLED issue skip already has a loop. While the issue is open, the nightly job runs the test. 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds, plus 14 quiet days, are the bar for closing the issue. Closing it removes the skip.

A code skip has no issue. The decorator is the only record, and it stays in force during `rerun-disabled-tests`. The nightly job cannot tell a fixed code skip from one that still fails.

This RFC leaves the issue path and the `rerun_disabled_tests` upload unchanged. Code-skip reruns go to a separate prefix, `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.

```
Python skip decorator
        ↓
mark safe-to-rerun skips
        ↓
pytest collection temporarily removes those skips
        ↓
test body passes, fails, or remains skipped
        ↓
JUnit XML retains the original skip reason
        ↓
results upload to rerun_disabled_code_skips
        ↓
test-infra can eventually propose deleting fixed decorators
```

Only code skips are marked safe to rerun. Capability skips are not marked.

Collection drops those marks for that job only. The decorator stays in the source file.

The body then passes, fails, or remains skipped. It remains skipped when a capability skip still applies. A pass or a fail does not edit the file.

The JUnit row keeps the original skip reason, so a pass or a fail can still be matched to the decorator that was lifted.

Those rows upload to `rerun_disabled_code_skips` and are not added to `rerun_disabled_tests`.

test-infra can later propose deleting decorators that clear the same bar as closing a DISABLED issue: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. There is no 14-day quiet period, because a code skip has no issue. https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026 is that last step. It would open one daily draft pull request. That draft does not merge.

## Goals

- Run code skips in `rerun-disabled-tests`.
- Leave capability skips skipped, on every platform.
- Keep the original skip reason on the result when the body passes or fails.
- Upload code-skip reruns only to `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.
- Leave `rerun_disabled_tests` unchanged.
- Propose decorator deletions in a later human-reviewed draft. Do not delete them here.

## Non-goals

- Deleting decorators in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916.
- Merging a deletion from https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026.
- Rerunning capability skips.
- Changing the DISABLED-issue path, its upload, or its 14 quiet days.
- Limiting the split to one platform.

## Alternatives

- Leave code skips until someone deletes them by hand. A fixed test stays skipped, with no green-run count behind a deletion.
- Upload code-skip reruns into `rerun_disabled_tests`. This RFC uses a separate prefix so the existing collection stays as it is.
- Rerun every skip. Failures on a machine that cannot run the test would be mixed in with real regressions.

## Additional context

- PyTorch: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026
- Deletion bar: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. No 14-day quiet period.

There is no 14-day quiet period, because a code skip has no issue. https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026 is that last step. It would open one daily draft pull request. That draft does not merge.

## Goals

- Run code skips in `rerun-disabled-tests`.
- Leave capability skips skipped, on every platform.
- Keep the original skip reason on the result when the body passes or fails.
- Upload code-skip reruns only to `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.
- Leave `rerun_disabled_tests` unchanged.
- Propose decorator deletions in a later human-reviewed draft. Do not delete them here.

## Non-goals

- Deleting decorators in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916.
- Merging a deletion from https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026.
- Rerunning capability skips.
- Changing the DISABLED-issue path, its upload, or its 14 quiet days.
- Limiting the split to one platform.

## Alternatives

- Leave code skips until someone deletes them by hand. A fixed test stays skipped, with no green-run count behind a deletion.
- Upload code-skip reruns into `rerun_disabled_tests`. This RFC uses a separate prefix so the existing collection stays as it is.
- Rerun every skip. Failures on a machine that cannot run the test would be mixed in with real regressions.

## Additional context

- PyTorch: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026
- Deletion bar: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. No 14-day quiet period.

import threading, time, torch
from torch.autograd.profiler import profile

@torch.jit.script
def foo(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    for _ in range(5):
        x = torch.mm(x, x).clamp(-1.0, 1.0)
    return x

@torch.jit.script
def bar(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.jit.Future[torch.Tensor]:
    return torch.jit._fork(foo, x)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
def log(msg):
    print(f"{(time.perf_counter()-t0)*1e3:8.1f} ms  tid={threading.get_ident()}  {msg}", flush=True)

def cb(f):
    log("callback start"); time.sleep(2.0); log("callback end")

x = torch.rand(256, 256)
with profile(use_kineto=True) as p:
    fut = bar(x)
    fut.add_done_callback(cb)
    fut.wait()
    log("wait returned")
log("profile exited")
time.sleep(5.0)

## Claude's analysis (based on code reading of `main` at 006c9f96a64):
The valgrind stacks point to an ordering problem in `INST(RET)` (`torch/csrc/jit/runtime/interpreter.cpp`, around L480-490). For the last frame, it calls `future_->markCompleted(...)` first and `leaveFrame()` afterwards.

- `markCompleted()` (`aten/src/ATen/core/ivalue_inl.h`, around L951-969) sets `completed_`, calls `finished_cv_.notify_all()` to wake threads blocked in `wait()`, and then runs the future's callbacks on the current thread before returning.
- `leaveFrame()` pops the frame. The frame owns `std::unique_ptr<at::RecordFunction> record_function` (`interpreter/frame.h`), so popping it runs `~RecordFunction()` -> `end()` -> the profiler's `onFunctionExitTLS()` -> `onFunctionExitImpl()`, which writes `end_time_` and `end_tid_` through the event pointer saved at begin.

So when the function runs on the interop thread pool, the waiting thread can wake up as soon as `markCompleted()` notifies it. That thread can then leave `profile()`. `disableProfiler()` -> `finalizeTrace()` -> `getRecords()` -> `materialize()` -> `op_events_.clear()` frees the event blocks. Only after that does the interop thread reach `leaveFrame()` and write into the freed event. In the repro, the sleeping done callback just keeps this window open. The profiler's TLS callback path has no protection against a late exit like this: `disableProfiler()` only drains in-flight callbacks for the global-callback path (`GlobalCallbackSession`).

A possible fix is to call `leaveFrame()` before `markCompleted()` in `INST(RET)`. `leaveFrame()` only touches `registers` and `frames`, so the outputs on `stack` are unaffected.

## Script:
```python
import threading, time, torch
from torch.autograd.profiler import profile

@torch.jit.script
def foo(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    for _ in range(5):
        x = torch.mm(x, x).clamp(-1.0, 1.0)
    return x

@torch.jit.script
def bar(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.jit.Future[torch.Tensor]:
    return torch.jit._fork(foo, x)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
def log(msg):
    print(f"{(time.perf_counter()-t0)*1e3:8.1f} ms  tid={threading.get_ident()}  {msg}", flush=True)

def cb(f):
    log("callback start"); time.sleep(2.0); log("callback end")

x = torch.rand(256, 256)
with profile(use_kineto=True) as p:
    fut = bar(x)
    fut.add_done_callback(cb)
    fut.wait()
    log("wait returned")
log("profile exited")
time.sleep(5.0)
```

## Claude's analysis (based on code reading of `main` at 006c9f96a64):
The valgrind stacks point to an ordering problem in `INST(RET)` (`torch/csrc/jit/runtime/interpreter.cpp`, around L480-490). For the last frame, it calls `future_->markCompleted(...)` first and `leaveFrame()` afterwards.

- `markCompleted()` (`aten/src/ATen/core/ivalue_inl.h`, around L951-969) sets `completed_`, calls `finished_cv_.notify_all()` to wake threads blocked in `wait()`, and then runs the future's callbacks on the current thread before returning.
- `leaveFrame()` pops the frame. The frame owns `std::unique_ptr<at::RecordFunction> record_function` (`interpreter/frame.h`), so popping it runs `~RecordFunction()` -> `end()` -> the profiler's `onFunctionExitTLS()` -> `onFunctionExitImpl()`, which writes `end_time_` and `end_tid_` through the event pointer saved at begin.

So when the function runs on the interop thread pool, the waiting thread can wake up as soon as `markCompleted()` notifies it. That thread can then leave `profile()`. `disableProfiler()` -> `finalizeTrace()` -> `getRecords()` -> `materialize()` -> `op_events_.clear()` frees the event blocks. Only after that does the interop thread reach `leaveFrame()` and write into the freed event. In the repro, the sleeping done callback just keeps this window open. The profiler's TLS callback path has no protection against a late exit like this: `disableProfiler()` only drains in-flight callbacks for the global-callback path (`GlobalCallbackSession`).

A possible fix is to call `leaveFrame()` before `markCompleted()` in `INST(RET)`. `leaveFrame()` only touches `registers` and `frames`, so the outputs on `stack` are unaffected.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On Python versions before 3.12, `torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()` with its default arguments drops one reference to `True` on every call. `True` is not an immortal object before Python 3.12 (PEP 683), so a process that takes many snapshots aborts after enough calls:

```
Fatal Python error: bool_dealloc: deallocating True or False: bug likely caused by a refcount error in a C extension
```

This is the same defect as #198372, which was found on Python 3.12 through `MemPool.snapshot()` with large pool IDs. Before Python 3.12, the default call is also affected, because the wrapper passes `(0, 0, include_traces)` and `True` and `0` are ordinary reference-counted objects there.

Reproduction (one CUDA GPU):

```python
import sys
import torch

torch.cuda.init()
before = sys.getrefcount(True)
for _ in range(1000):
    torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()
print(sys.getrefcount(True) - before)
```

Expected: `0`. Observed with torch 2.13.0 on Python 3.11.7: `-1000` (one reference per call). `torch._C._cuda_memorySnapshot(None)`, which does not pass a tuple, shows no change.

Cause: `THCPModule_memorySnapshot` in `torch/csrc/cuda/Module.cpp` wraps the borrowed items from `PyTuple_GetItem` in an owning `THPObjectPtr`, so each call decrements every element of the argument tuple. #199044 (commit 9d9880802d) fixes this on main. The v2.14.1 source still contains the old code.

Request: please consider the fix in #199044 for the next 2.14 patch release. Any library that calls `torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()` per operation (for example, to plan memory before a kernel launch) crashes long-running processes on Python 3.10 and 3.11.

Workaround for affected versions: call `torch._C._cuda_memorySnapshot(None)["segments"]` instead of `torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()`.

### Versions

- PyTorch 2.13.0+cu126 (observed); v2.14.1 (same code by source inspection)
- Python 3.11.7
- Linux (RHEL 8), NVIDIA A100 64GB, CUDA 12.6

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

[#198333](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/198333) was closed by
[#198680](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198680), which turned `use_rand4x` off by
default. The underlying offset reconstruction was not changed, and no behavioural test was
added. `torch/_inductor/config.py` still reads:

```python
# Use tl.rand4x/randn4x for 1D CUDA Triton random. Disabled pending
# https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/198333
use_rand4x = os.environ.get("TORCHINDUCTOR_USE_RAND4X") == "1"
```

"Disabled pending" implies the path is meant to come back. The path *is* covered by three
tests in `test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py`, but all three assert **codegen and shape
only** — which generator the kernel emits, and that the output has the expected shape:

| test | assertion |
|---|---|
| `test_randn_uses_randn4x` | `code.count("triton_helpers.randn4x") == 1` |
| `test_rand4x_falls_back_in_reduction` | `rand4x` absent, `tl.rand` present |
| `test_align_random_eager_skips_rand4x` | the flag suppresses `rand4x` |

None of them asserts anything about the *values* the path produces, or about two kernels in
one program agreeing. That is, I think, exactly why this shipped for three and a half months:
the tests confirmed `rand4x` was wired up, never that it was correct. So whoever re-enables
the default still gets no signal from a numerical mistake.

### Still reproducible on main

On `2.16.0.dev20261014+cu130` / triton 3.9.0, RTX 5090 (sm_120), setting the documented
environment variable silently corrupts gradients under activation checkpointing:

| `use_rand4x` | forward/recompute dropout mask agreement |
|---|---|
| `False` (shipped default) | 100.000% |
| `True` via `TORCHINDUCTOR_USE_RAND4X=1` | **50.020%** |

Eager is 100.000% in both. 50% is what two independent masks give at p=0.5, so the backward is
differentiating a mask the forward never applied. No exception, no NaN, no warning.

This is not an eager-vs-compiled comparison, so `fallback_random` does not apply. The invariant
is inside a single compiled program: its forward and its own checkpoint recompute must realize
the same mask. Setting `fallback_random=True` masks the defect rather than exposing it, because
it forces the eager RNG path and the 4x path is then never taken.

Same on the originally affected release, `2.13.0+cu130` / triton 3.7.1, where the path is
unconditional — and on two architectures:

| GPU | arch | agreement, as shipped | with `_can_use_4x_random()` forced `False` |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 5090 | sm_120, 170 SMs | 49.999% | 100.000% |
| A100-SXM4-80GB | sm_80, 108 SMs | 49.999% | 100.000% |

### Mechanism

Not that `rand4x` computes wrong numbers. `tl.rand` draws one Philox output per counter over
`BLOCK` counters; `rand4x` draws all four over `BLOCK/4`. They are different streams by
construction, which is fine as long as one logical dropout consistently uses one of them.

It does not. `_can_use_4x_random()` selects `rand4x` only for a 1-D kernel, and under
checkpointing the two halves are codegen'd differently. Measured per kernel body, identically
on both GPUs, with shape `(8, 64, 4096)` fed through `.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()`:

| kernel | dims | generator |
|---|---|---|
| `triton_poi_fused_clone_native_dropout_transpose_0` (forward) | 2-D | `tl.rand` |
| `triton_poi_fused_native_dropout_native_dropout_backward_0` (recompute) | 1-D | **`rand4x`** |

Forcing `_can_use_4x_random()` to `False` puts both on `tl.rand` and agreement returns to
100.000%.

### What I could not reproduce

#198333 also reported 100.000% channel-group duplication in the forward under `no_grad`. I did
**not** see it: duplication is ~49.99% (i.e. correct) on both GPUs, at the reported shape and at
8 shapes in a sweep, and `rand4x` is never called in the forward in any of them because that
kernel fuses 2-D. The original report was on an RTX PRO 6000, also sm_120, with the kernel roles
reversed. **I cannot explain the difference** — I checked whether the 1-D/2-D choice depends on
device properties and it does not; `triton_tensor_ndim()` is computed from the range trees at
codegen time. So this is "not reproduced here, cause unknown", not a claim that the report was
wrong. It does suggest a fix validated on a single GPU may not be sufficient.

### Proposed change

One test method, no source changes. I put it in
`test/inductor/test_dropout_align_random_eager.py` because that file is CUDA-only and already
has the seeding and mask helpers, but the three existing `use_rand4x` tests live in
`test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py` and I am happy to move it there instead. It
asserts the program-level invariant — the recompute must realize the mask the forward applied —
under `@config.patch(align_random_eager=False, use_rand4x=True)`.

Because the path is currently broken on purpose, it carries `@unittest.expectedFailure`, the
idiom already used for three tests in that file. So it is green today, and when the
reconstruction is fixed it XPASSes and CI goes red — which is the prompt to drop the decorator
and flip the default back. Verified both ways: it fails at ratio 0.499651 with the flag on,
passes with it off, and the full 14-test file reports `OK (expected failures=4)`.

I deliberately did **not** write a test for the duplication symptom. Whether it appears depends
on how Inductor fuses the forward, which varies between machines, and a test that flaky is worse
than none.

### Ask

If this is worth having, please mark it `actionable` and I will send the test-only PR.

### Agent details

This investigation and this write-up were prepared with AI assistance (Claude). The agent
localized the mechanism, wrote the measurement script and drafted this text; I ran the
reproductions, reviewed the test line by line, and I am responsible for its accuracy. The
measurements are reproducible from the script and the versions named above. The AI-assisted
analysis of #198333 that I am citing is the original reporter's, not mine.

### Error logs

_No response_

{"repository": "pytorch/pytorch", "task_candidate_id": 21875, "repository_id": 236, "issue_number": 201046, "github_issue_id": 5865628395, "html_url": "https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201046", "created_at": "2026-10-15T11:56:05+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "No behavioural test guards the use_rand4x re-enable (#198333 was disabled, not fixed)", "body_text": "### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

[#198333](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/198333) was closed by
[#198680](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/198680), which turned `use_rand4x` off by
default. The underlying offset reconstruction was not changed, and no behavioural test was
added. `torch/_inductor/config.py` still reads:

```python
# Use tl.rand4x/randn4x for 1D CUDA Triton random. Disabled pending
# https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/198333
use_rand4x = os.environ.get("TORCHINDUCTOR_USE_RAND4X") == "1"
```

"Disabled pending" implies the path is meant to come back. The path *is* covered by three
tests in `test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py`, but all three assert **codegen and shape
only** — which generator the kernel emits, and that the output has the expected shape:

| test | assertion |
|---|---|
| `test_randn_uses_randn4x` | `code.count("triton_helpers.randn4x") == 1` |
| `test_rand4x_falls_back_in_reduction` | `rand4x` absent, `tl.rand` present |
| `test_align_random_eager_skips_rand4x` | the flag suppresses `rand4x` |

None of them asserts anything about the *values* the path produces, or about two kernels in
one program agreeing. That is, I think, exactly why this shipped for three and a half months:
the tests confirmed `rand4x` was wired up, never that it was correct. So whoever re-enables
the default still gets no signal from a numerical mistake.

### Still reproducible on main

On `2.16.0.dev20261014+cu130` / triton 3.9.0, RTX 5090 (sm_120), setting the documented
environment variable silently corrupts gradients under activation checkpointing:

| `use_rand4x` | forward/recompute dropout mask agreement |
|---|---|
| `False` (shipped default) | 100.000% |
| `True` via `TORCHINDUCTOR_USE_RAND4X=1` | **50.020%** |

Eager is 100.000% in both. 50% is what two independent masks give at p=0.5, so the backward is
differentiating a mask the forward never applied. No exception, no NaN, no warning.

This is not an eager-vs-compiled comparison, so `fallback_random` does not apply. The invariant
is inside a single compiled program: its forward and its own checkpoint recompute must realize
the same mask. Setting `fallback_random=True` masks the defect rather than exposing it, because
it forces the eager RNG path and the 4x path is then never taken.

Same on the originally affected release, `2.13.0+cu130` / triton 3.7.1, where the path is
unconditional — and on two architectures:

| GPU | arch | agreement, as shipped | with `_can_use_4x_random()` forced `False` |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 5090 | sm_120, 170 SMs | 49.999% | 100.000% |
| A100-SXM4-80GB | sm_80, 108 SMs | 49.999% | 100.000% |

### Mechanism

Not that `rand4x` computes wrong numbers. `tl.rand` draws one Philox output per counter over
`BLOCK` counters; `rand4x` draws all four over `BLOCK/4`. They are different streams by
construction, which is fine as long as one logical dropout consistently uses one of them.

It does not. `_can_use_4x_random()` selects `rand4x` only for a 1-D kernel, and under
checkpointing the two halves are codegen'd differently. Measured per kernel body, identically
on both GPUs, with shape `(8, 64, 4096)` fed through `.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()`:

| kernel | dims | generator |
|---|---|---|
| `triton_poi_fused_clone_native_dropout_transpose_0` (forward) | 2-D | `tl.rand` |
| `triton_poi_fused_native_dropout_native_dropout_backward_0` (recompute) | 1-D | **`rand4x`** |

Forcing `_can_use_4x_random()` to `False` puts both on `tl.rand` and agreement returns to
100.000%.

### What I could not reproduce

#198333 also reported 100.000% channel-group duplication in the forward under `no_grad`. I did
**not** see it: duplication is ~49.99% (i.e. correct) on both GPUs, at the reported shape and at
8 shapes in a sweep, and `rand4x` is never called in the forward in any of them because that
kernel fuses 2-D. The original report was on an RTX PRO 6000, also sm_120, with the kernel roles
reversed. **I cannot explain the difference** — I checked whether the 1-D/2-D choice depends on
device properties and it does not; `triton_tensor_ndim()` is computed from the range trees at
codegen time. So this is "not reproduced here, cause unknown", not a claim that the report was
wrong. It does suggest a fix validated on a single GPU may not be sufficient.

### Proposed change

One test method, no source changes. I put it in
`test/inductor/test_dropout_align_random_eager.py` because that file is CUDA-only and already
has the seeding and mask helpers, but the three existing `use_rand4x` tests live in
`test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py` and I am happy to move it there instead. It
asserts the program-level invariant — the recompute must realize the mask the forward applied —
under `@config.patch(align_random_eager=False, use_rand4x=True)`.

Because the path is currently broken on purpose, it carries `@unittest.expectedFailure`, the
idiom already used for three tests in that file. So it is green today, and when the
reconstruction is fixed it XPASSes and CI goes red — which is the prompt to drop the decorator
and flip the default back. Verified both ways: it fails at ratio 0.499651 with the flag on,
passes with it off, and the full 14-test file reports `OK (expected failures=4)`.

I deliberately did **not** write a test for the duplication symptom. Whether it appears depends
on how Inductor fuses the forward, which varies between machines, and a test that flaky is worse
than none.

### Ask

If this is worth having, please mark it `actionable` and I will send the test-only PR.

### Agent details

This investigation and this write-up were prepared with AI assistance (Claude). The agent
localized the mechanism, wrote the measurement script and drafted this text; I ran the
reproductions, reviewed the test line by line, and I am responsible for its accuracy. The
measurements are reproducible from the script and the versions named above. The AI-assisted
analysis of #198333 that I am citing is the original reporter's, not mine.

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I hit this exporting robot policies (ACT) with ExecuTorch’s CUDA backend on Jetson Thor, which sends every convolution through these templates, so our convs ran in full FP32.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> Since #173731 (in 2.11), the forward conv2d, conv3d and transposed-conv Triton templates in `torch/_inductor/kernel/conv.py` set `ALLOW_TF32` from `torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision`, the cuDNN-wide setting, whose default is `"none"`. Eager convolutions follow `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision`, whose default is `"tf32"`, and 2.10's templates read `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32`, whose default is `True`. So with default settings a max-autotune conv template now computes in full FP32 where eager uses TF32, and setting `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision` does not change it. The two backward conv templates still read the legacy `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32`, and the FX graph cache key does not include the convolution setting.
>
> In this reproducer's autotuning on a Jetson AGX Thor, the fastest conv template took 0.095 ms with `ALLOW_TF32=False`, and 0.036 ms with the fix below, which compiles the templates with `ALLOW_TF32 : tl.constexpr = True`.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:inductor-conv-template-tf32](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:inductor-conv-template-tf32): all five templates read `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision`, and the setting is added to the FX graph cache key. It will be sent as a PR once this issue is triaged.

Reproducer:

```python
import torch
import torch._inductor.utils
from torch._inductor import config
from torch._inductor.utils import run_and_get_code

# Inductor autotunes templates only on GPUs with at least 68 SMs; this line
# is needed on smaller ones (the run below is on a 20-SM Jetson Thor).
torch._inductor.utils.is_big_gpu = lambda *args: True

m = torch.nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1, bias=False).cuda()
x = torch.randn(2, 32, 28, 28, device="cuda")
print("torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision =", torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision)
print("torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision =", torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision)
with config.patch(max_autotune=True, max_autotune_conv_backends="TRITON"), torch.no_grad():
    _, code = run_and_get_code(torch.compile(m), x)
print(*sorted({line.strip() for line in code[0].splitlines() if line.strip().startswith("ALLOW_TF32")}), sep="\n")
```

Output:

```
torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = tf32
torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision = none
ALLOW_TF32 : tl.constexpr = False
```

### Error logs

No error: the generated template has `ALLOW_TF32 : tl.constexpr = False` although eager convolutions use TF32 under the same settings.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> Since #173731 (in 2.11), the forward conv2d, conv3d and transposed-conv Triton templates in `torch/_inductor/kernel/conv.py` set `ALLOW_TF32` from `torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision`, the cuDNN-wide setting, whose default is `"none"`. Eager convolutions follow `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision`, whose default is `"tf32"`, and 2.10's templates read `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32`, whose default is `True`. So with default settings a max-autotune conv template now computes in full FP32 where eager uses TF32, and setting `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision` does not change it. The two backward conv templates still read the legacy `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32`, and the FX graph cache key does not include the convolution setting.
>
> In this reproducer's autotuning on a Jetson AGX Thor, the fastest conv template took 0.095 ms with `ALLOW_TF32=False`, and 0.036 ms with the fix below, which compiles the templates with `ALLOW_TF32 : tl.constexpr = True`.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:inductor-conv-template-tf32](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:inductor-conv-template-tf32): all five templates read `torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision`, and the setting is added to the FX graph cache key. torch._inductor.utils.is_big_gpu = lambda *args: True

m = torch.nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1, bias=False).cuda()
x = torch.randn(2, 32, 28, 28, device="cuda")
print("torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision =", torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision)

body_text:
I was looking at a case where a finite KL penalty unexpectedly becomes an infinite loss and gradient, which could disrupt optimization in some experiments. I can also work on a small formalization with TorchLean if that would be helpful :)

## AI-generated analysis and reproduction

`kl_divergence(Normal(...), Normal(...))` returns an infinite loss and gradient in this case, although finite values fit in the input dtype:

```python
import torch

scale = torch.tensor(1e-4, dtype=torch.float16, requires_grad=True)
p = torch.distributions.Normal(torch.zeros_like(scale), scale)
q = torch.distributions.Normal(torch.zeros_like(scale), torch.ones_like(scale))
loss = torch.distributions.kl_divergence(p, q)
gradient, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, scale)

reference_scale = scale.detach().double()
reference = (reference_scale.square() - 1) / 2 - reference_scale.log()
print("loss:", loss.detach().item(), "gradient:", gradient.item())
print("float64 reference:", reference.item())
print("reference gradient:", (reference_scale - 1 / reference_scale).item())
```

Output on CPU:

```text
loss: inf gradient: -inf
float64 reference: 8.710174451413195
reference gradient: -9998.34078198579
```

`_kl_normal_normal` squares the scale ratio before taking its logarithm. The square rounds to zero here, although both scales are positive. Computing the logarithmic term from the scales separately avoids that underflow. Smaller positive scales also reproduce this in float32 and float64.

The finite reference uses the actual stored float16 scale, not the decimal literal before rounding.

### Versions

Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; the reproduction runs on CPU.

Also reproduced with `_kl_normal_normal` extracted from commit `215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8`. Its implementation is unchanged in commit [`514f3f72bf9427d201e934ecec25048c4e678ff1`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/514f3f72bf9427d201e934ecec25048c4e678ff1/torch/distributions/kl.py), checked on October 15, 2026.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Build:** `torch 2.16.0.dev20261013+cu130` (nightly, git `ca883d596dd5c0ce182976ed979d69d167ad706c`), Python 3.12.
Reproduces on CPU (`aot_eager`, `inductor`) and on CUDA (`inductor`, B200). `backend="eager"` is correct.
## Symptom
A module mutates a buffer in place in `forward` (a step counter) and scales its output by a value computed from that buffer. Under `torch.compile`:
- the forward output matches eager;
- the buffer ends up with the right value;
- **the parameter gradients are wrong, with no error or warning** (1.5x in this repro; the factor depends on the formula).
## Run
```bash
python buffer_mutation_bw_recompute.py
```
Output on the build above:
```
eager      forward_matches=True buffer_matches=True weight_grad_ratio=1.0000
aot_eager  forward_matches=True buffer_matches=True weight_grad_ratio=1.5000
inductor   forward_matches=True buffer_matches=True weight_grad_ratio=1.5000
```
To see the graphs: `TORCH_LOGS=aot_graphs python buffer_mutation_bw_recompute.py`
## What happens (from `TORCH_LOGS=aot_graphs`, aot_eager)
Forward graph (excerpt):
```
add: "f32[][]" = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(primals_1, 1)        # n + 1  (the mutation)
add_1 = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(add, 1)                        # (n + 1) + 1
div = torch.ops.aten.div.Tensor(add_1, 20)
clamp = torch.ops.aten.clamp.default(div, None, 1.0)             # scale = 0.1
mul = torch.ops.aten.mul.Tensor(addmm, clamp)
copy_ = torch.ops.aten.copy_.default(primals_1, add)             # buffer mutated in-graph
return (mul, primals_1, primals_4)                                # saves primals_1 (the buffer)
```
Backward graph (excerpt):
```
add = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(primals_1, 1)    # recomputed from the ALREADY-MUTATED buffer (n = 1)
add_1 = torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor(add, 1)
div = torch.ops.aten.div.Tensor(add_1, 20)
clamp = torch.ops.aten.clamp.default(div, None, 1.0)   # scale = 0.15 instead of 0.1
mul_1 = torch.ops.aten.mul.Tensor(tangents_1, clamp)
```
The partitioner saves the graph input `primals_1` (the buffer) and recomputes `scale` in the backward. But the forward graph itself mutates `primals_1` in place (`copy_(primals_1, add)`; `keep_input_mutations=True`, `mutates_data=True`). By the time the backward runs, the saved input holds the **post-mutation** value. No version-counter error fires, because the mutation happens inside the compiled forward before the tensor is saved for backward (`saved_tensor_is_graph_input=[True, True]`).
## Variants tried (all wrong, ratio 1.5 under aot_eager)
| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| `self.n.add_(1)`, then read `self.n` | wrong |
| out of place: `n = self.n + 1; self.n.copy_(n)`, use `n` | wrong |
| `n = self.n.clone()` before mutating, use `n` | wrong |
| read the buffer first, mutate after the use | wrong |
| `torch._functorch.config.activation_memory_budget = 1.0` | wrong |
| compute the buffer-derived scale outside the compiled region and pass it in as an input | **correct** (workaround) |
## Likely fix direction
The min-cut partitioner should not recompute backward values from graph inputs that the forward mutates in place (inputs with `mutates_data=True` under `keep_input_mutations`). It should save the needed activation (here `clamp`, a 0-d tensor), or a pre-mutation copy of the input, instead.
## Repro script: `buffer_mutation_bw_recompute.py`
```python
"""torch.compile gives silently wrong gradients when the forward mutates a buffer.
The backward recomputes a buffer-derived value from the buffer *after* the
compiled forward has already mutated it in place.
"""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
class Counter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin = nn.Linear(4, 4)
        self.register_buffer("n", torch.zeros(()))
    def forward(self, x):
        self.n.add_(1)
        scale = torch.clamp((self.n + 1) / 20, max=1.0)
        return self.lin(x) * scale
def run(backend):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = Counter()
    x = torch.randn(2, 4)
    f = m
    if backend is not None:
        f = torch.compile(m, backend=backend, fullgraph=True)
    out = f(x)
    out.sum().backward()
    return out.detach(), m.lin.weight.grad.clone(), m.n.item()
torch._dynamo.reset()
out_ref, grad_ref, n_ref = run(None)
for backend in ("eager", "aot_eager", "inductor"):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    out, grad, n = run(backend)
    print(
        f"{backend:10s} "
        f"forward_matches={torch.allclose(out, out_ref)} "
        f"buffer_matches={n == n_ref} "
        f"weight_grad_ratio={(grad / grad_ref).mean().item():.4f}"
    )
```

body_text:
### Summary

`ProcessGroupNCCL` currently disables NCCL’s NVLS algorithm whenever deterministic algorithms are enabled and the user has not explicitly set `NCCL_ALGO`:

[https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp#L1010-L1025](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp#L1010-L1025)

This restriction can now be relaxed, provided the qualification requirements described below are met. NVLink SHARP reductions use deterministic reduction ordering and rounding on qualified hardware and software stacks, and the required driver and other software components must be present.

### Current behavior

When `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` is active, `ProcessGroupNCCL` sets:

```text
NCCL_ALGO=^NVLS
```

This prevents NCCL from selecting NVLS, including on systems where the NVLS reduction path is deterministic. It can unnecessarily reduce collective performance on Hopper, Blackwell, and newer NVSwitch systems.

The restriction is also inconsistent with an explicitly supplied `NCCL_ALGO`, which PyTorch currently leaves unchanged.

### Updated determinism qualification

The applicable guarantee is same-setup bitwise repeatability: identical input bits and an unchanged execution plan and numerical environment produce identical result bits.

- Blackwell and later NVLS reductions are deterministic for an identical qualified configuration.
- Hopper NVLS reductions are deterministic on a qualified driver and firmware stack when the participating physical GPU set remains fixed. This includes process restarts and ordinary GPU virtual-address changes.
- Hopper does not guarantee identical bits when the participating physical GPU subset changes. That is a different effective execution plan, rather than nondeterminism within the same plan.
- NVIDIA identifies the Hopper fix with an R550 driver update. For initial deployment, use Linux `>=570.26` or Windows `>=570.65`.

### Proposed change

Replace the blanket NVLS exclusion with a capability-based policy:

1. Do not disable NVLS in deterministic mode on Blackwell and later.
2. Allow NVLS on Hopper when the runtime satisfies the qualified driver boundary. Initially, use a conservative CUDA 12.8/R570-or-newer requirement unless NVIDIA provides an earlier exact R550 patch-level boundary.
3. Continue disabling NVLS on unqualified Hopper stacks and older architectures.
4. Preserve the existing behavior when the user explicitly sets `NCCL_ALGO`.
5. Log whether NVLS was retained or disabled and the architecture/driver condition that determined the result.

If reliably checking the full Hopper firmware qualification from PyTorch is not possible, an acceptable first step would be:

- enable NVLS unconditionally on Blackwell and later; and
- retain the existing Hopper restriction until the public qualification boundary is precise.

### Acceptance criteria

- Deterministic mode no longer sets `NCCL_ALGO=^NVLS` on qualified systems.
- Unqualified systems retain the current safe fallback.
- User-provided `NCCL_ALGO` values remain untouched.
- Tests cover the architecture and driver-version branches.
- Documentation states that determinism is guaranteed for a fixed participating physical GPU set and execution plan, not across different GPU subsets or algorithm choices.
- The obsolete “remove this once NVLS supports deterministic mode” comment and nondeterminism warning are updated.

### Motivation

NVLS is a major performance path for collectives on NVSwitch systems. Disabling it globally is no longer necessary on qualified platforms and imposes a performance penalty on users who request deterministic execution.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With PDL enabled (`TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL=1`), `torch.compile` raises `CannotStaticallyLaunchKernel: static launch does not support launch attributes` when `strict_static_triton_launcher` is set. Without the strict flag, compilation succeeds but the static launcher is not used, and the static launcher, FX graph cache and autotune cache tests fail.

MRE:

```python
import torch

torch._inductor.config.triton.enable_pdl = True
torch._inductor.config.strict_static_triton_launcher = True

@torch.compile
def f(x, y):
    return x + y

x = torch.randn(10, device="cuda")
f(x, x)
```

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: CannotStaticallyLaunchKernel: static launch does not support launch attributes
```

Several PyTorch tests are failing when launched with `TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL=1`:

```
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestStaticTritonCompileResult::test_any
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestStaticTritonCompileResult::test_basic_compile
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestStaticTritonCompileResult::test_custom_op_bad_fake_dtype_fails_fast
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestStaticTritonCompileResult::test_empty_tensor
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestFastCudaLauncherCompileResult::test_basic_compile
- test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py::TestFastCudaLauncherCompileResult::test_disable_fast_launcher
- test/inductor/test_codecache.py::TestFxGraphCache::test_cache_load_function_device_cuda_bfloat16_dynamic_False_bundle_triton_True_use_static_triton_launcher_True_grad_False
- test/inductor/test_codecache.py::TestFxGraphCache::test_cache_load_function_device_cuda_bfloat16_dynamic_False_bundle_triton_True_use_static_triton_launcher_True_grad_True
- test/inductor/test_codecache.py::TestFxGraphCache::test_cache_load_function_device_cuda_bfloat16_dynamic_True_bundle_triton_True_use_static_triton_launcher_True_grad_False
- test/inductor/test_codecache.py::TestFxGraphCache::test_cache_load_function_device_cuda_bfloat16_dynamic_True_bundle_triton_True_use_static_triton_launcher_True_grad_True

``` 

Example Repro CMD : ``TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL=1 python -m pytest -q test/inductor/test_static_triton_launcher.py``

I think static launcher should support PDL by launching with `cuLaunchKernelEx` and the programmatic stream serialization attribute, like AOTI does.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With PDL enabled (`TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL=1`) and `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, calling a compiled function raises `InterpreterError` from the generated kernel's `tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()` call. The same script works with PDL disabled.

MRE:

```python
import os

os.environ["TRITON_INTERPRET"] = "1"
os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL"] = "1"

import torch

@torch.compile
def f(x):
    return x + 1

f(torch.rand(256, device="cuda"))
```

```
  File "/tmp/tmpnvetjhlj/sx/csx6piiiz7qfhyabxxvxs7tnxobb7f425nej4xtnomzdzjbnyp6p.py", line 24, in triton_poi_fused_add_0
    tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()
...
triton.runtime.errors.InterpreterError: ValueError('Did you forget to add @triton.jit ? (`_semantic` argument must be provided outside of JIT functions.)')
```

One torch inductor test is failing with this issue:

```
- test/inductor/test_cuda_repro.py::CudaReproTests::test_triton_interpret
```

Repro command : `TORCHINDUCTOR_ENABLE_PDL=1 python -m pytest -q test/inductor/test_cuda_repro.py::CudaReproTests::test_triton_interpret`

Can be fixed by not emitting the PDL calls (or launch with PDL) when `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.distributed.checkpoint.save` treats a value under the same key on every rank as replicated. It keeps only one rank's copy and drops the others (see #120356). When the value is per-rank state, for example Python or NumPy RNG state, every rank restores that one copy on load, and the other ranks' state is lost.

In the example below, each rank seeds Python's `random` with `1234 + rank` and saves its state under the key `rng`. After loading, all four ranks restore rank 0's state.

```python
import os, random, tempfile
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
import torch.multiprocessing as mp


def run(rank, path):
    os.environ.update(MASTER_ADDR="localhost", MASTER_PORT="29513")
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=4)
    random.seed(1234 + rank)

    dcp.save({"rng": random.getstate()}, checkpoint_id=path)
    expected = random.random() 

    state = {"rng": random.getstate()}
    dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id=path)
    random.setstate(state["rng"])
    got = random.random()

    print(f"rank {rank}: expected {expected:.4f}  got {got:.4f}", flush=True)
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.spawn(run, args=(tempfile.mkdtemp(),), nprocs=4)
```

Output:

```
rank 0: expected 0.9665  got 0.9665
rank 1: expected 0.9086  got 0.9665
rank 2: expected 0.5334  got 0.9665
rank 3: expected 0.1487  got 0.9665
```

#### Why this matters

Saving RNG state is meant to make a resumed run continue exactly like an uninterrupted one. However, when every rank's RNG state collapses to one rank's, exact continuation no longer holds. RLinf ran into this problem and fixed it in RLinf/RLinf#1570. They report that their original checkpoint "restored incorrect rank RNG streams and diverged during continuation".

Also, in some setups, ranks are seeded differently so that dropout masks or MoE router noise are independent across ranks. After the collapse, all ranks draw the same values, so this independence is lost. For example, Megatron-LM seeds its RNG per rank for independent MoE router noise. NVIDIA/Megatron-LM#6858 fixed a resume that restored other ranks' streams in its own checkpoint format, and left a TODO for the same defect in its `fsdp_dtensor` format, which saves with `dcp.save`([source](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/3914483fd325e053797aff3fa431d4a3141139aa/megatron/training/checkpointing.py#L573-L577)).

#### Where it happens

When building its save plan, every rank adds a write request for each value, so every rank asks to write `rng`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/default_planner.py#L555-L559

The coordinator then removes duplicates in `dedup_save_plans`. It groups requests by key alone and keeps only one rank's request for each key:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/_dedup_save_plans.py#L36-L55

#### Expected behavior

1. Warn when values under the same key differ across ranks. Each rank could hash its non-tensor values while building its local plan. The hashes would travel with the local plans that are already gathered on the coordinator, so the coordinator could compare them cheaply.
2. Document the requirement. The documentation should state that values under the same key must be identical on every rank.

### Versions

Reproduced on torch 2.14.1 (stable) and 2.15.0.dev20260923 (nightly, 54b9926e).

### 🐛 Describe the bug

While adding `torch.compile` coverage to TensorDict's CI, I noticed that in-place math on one of our types compiles on torch 2.14.1 but fails on the 2.15.0 release candidate (pytorch/tensordict#2787). Chasing that down the rabbit hole led me to believe that the issue is actually in Dynamo: inside compiled code, a function's `__name__` now comes from its code object, so a name set by `functools.wraps` is lost. TensorDict happened to get an `AttributeError` out of it, but in general nothing errors, and the compiled code just uses the wrong string.

I think this should be fixed before 2.15.0 ships, since it's a silent wrong result, and plenty of code dispatches on or logs `fn.__name__`. Expected behavior is that compiled code sees the same `__name__` as eager, as it does on 2.14.1.

```python
import functools
import torch

def deco(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def new_func(x):
        return func(x)
    return new_func

@deco
def add_(x):
    return x + 1

def f(x, method=add_):
    return x + len(method.__name__)

x = torch.zeros(1)
print(f(x))                                 # tensor([4.]), len("add_")
print(torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True)(x))  # tensor([8.]) on 2.15.0, len("new_func")
```

I had an agent investigate further; below is the AI-assisted analysis.

### Error logs

None. The compiled function returns a different value, with no error and no graph break.

### AI-assisted analysis

An AI coding agent (Claude, in the Pi harness) bisected the nightlies and read the Dynamo source at my request. I reviewed its findings before filing.

> Bisected on the CPU nightlies with the script above: 2.15.0.dev20260903 (7c31c89) is the last good build, and 2.15.0.dev20260904 (3780801) the first bad one.
>
> In that window, #193983 ("Model readonly members by making `setter` a required arg in `Member`") removed the `_fn_getattr` getters of `UserFunctionVariable` for `__name__`, `__qualname__`, `__code__`, `__defaults__`, `__kwdefaults__`, `__annotations__`, `__type_params__`, `__doc__`, `__module__` and `__closure__`. These attributes now come from `BaseUserFunctionVariable.tp_getset` in `torch/_dynamo/variables/functions.py`, whose `__name__` getter calls `get_name()`, which returns `self.get_code().co_name`.
>
> The same check for each attribute that `functools.wraps` copies, or that can be assigned on a plain function:
>
> | Attribute | 2.14.1 | 2.15.0 RC and nightly 2.16.0.dev20261015 |
> |---|---|---|
> | `__name__`, from `functools.wraps` or assigned | eager value | the name of the code object |
> | `__doc__`, from `functools.wraps` or assigned | eager value | `None` |
> | `__module__`, assigned | eager value | the module of the function's globals |
> | `__qualname__`, from `functools.wraps` or assigned | already wrong | wrong |
>
> `backend="eager"` gives the same results, so the bug is in Dynamo, not Inductor. The open PR #196887 reads `__name__` and `__qualname__` from the function object again, which would fix those two, but not `__doc__` or `__module__`.

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Compiling the backward of a function that runs on two side streams fails in Inductor's memory planner:

```python
import torch

def fn(x, y):
    s1 = torch.Stream(device="cuda")
    s2 = torch.Stream(device="cuda")
    with s1:
        a = 2 * x + y
    with s2:
        b = 2 * x + y
    return a, b

x = torch.ones(2, 2, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
y = torch.ones(2, 2, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
a, b = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)(x, y)
b.sum().backward()
```

The same program works with `backend="aot_eager"` and with a single side stream.

#### AI-generated analysis

> The four backward inputs Inductor complains about (`mul`, `add`, `mul_1`, `add_1`) are forward activations that no backward op computes with. They're saved only because the backward's sync ops list them as ordering deps: when `wrap_all_sync_nodes_with_control_deps` runs on the joint graph, the forward nodes on a stream are still in that stream's pending list when the backward `record_event`/`wait_event` on the same stream is wrapped, so they land in its `control_deps` `additional_deps`. The partitioner then saves them for the backward. Backward graph (`aot_eager`), abbreviated:
>
> ```
> control_deps = control_deps((mul, add, mul_3, add_2), subgraph_record_event_default, mul_3, add_2)
> control_deps_1 = control_deps((control_deps, mul_1, add_1, mul_2, getitem, getitem_1), subgraph_wait_event_default, ...)
> ```
>
> Inductor's `control_deps` lowering records those deps as `additional_buffer_deps`, which don't make the subgraph op a successor of the input buffer in memory planning, so `compute_memory_timeline` sees a freeable input buffer with no reader and asserts. Listing the input buffers with no successor nodes at the assertion gives exactly those four.
>
> Two possible fixes: don't add forward nodes as ordering deps of backward syncs (the forward graph has already run by then, and stream order already puts the backward sync after the forward work on that stream, so the edge adds nothing but forces saving the activations), and/or have the memory planner treat ordering-only uses as reads.

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With autograd enabled, a function that runs some work on the default stream and
some on a side stream compiles under Inductor, but the compiled forward fails
when called:

```python
import torch

def fn(x, y):
    s = torch.Stream(device="cuda")
    a = 2 * x + y
    with s:
        b = 2 * x + y
    return a, b

x = torch.ones(2, 2, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
y = torch.ones(2, 2, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
a, b = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)(x, y)
b.sum().backward()
```

It works with `backend="aot_eager"`, and with Inductor when the inputs don't require grad.

#### AI-generated analysis

> The compiled forward fetches a stream for its default-stream kernels with `_get_stream_by_index(2)`, but slot 2 of the external object registry (`torch._dynamo.graph_bytecode_inputs`) holds a `torch.Event`. Registry contents at the failing call, by type: `[Stream, Stream, Event, Stream, Event, Stream]`. The events and extra streams are registered while AOT autograd inserts the backward's stream syncs. Without autograd the registry is `[Stream, Stream]`, and the forward only fetches index 1 (the side stream) and runs the default-stream kernel on the current stream.
>
> The forward graph Inductor receives has no stream annotation on the default-stream nodes (only the side-stream nodes carry `{'stream': 1}`), so the index 2 is chosen somewhere in Inductor's training-path stream handling. I haven't found where.

### Describe the bug

On MPS, `torch.index_reduce` with `reduce="amax"` or `"amin"` does not propagate NaNs for `torch.float16` and `torch.float32`. `torch.bfloat16` behaves correctly.

The observation is that, given an array with `NaN` present,
1. CPU always returns `NaN`
2. MPS returns a finite value within the array OR the reduction identity (i.e. `-inf` or `+inf`) depending on the argument `include_self: bool` (`True` and `False` respectively).

To reproduce:

```python
import torch

print(torch.__version__)
print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available())

cases = (
    (float("nan"), 1.0, True),
    (1.0, float("nan"), True),
    (1.0, float("nan"), False),
)

for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.float32, torch.bfloat16):
    for reduce in ("amax", "amin"):
        for base, src, include_self in cases:
            outputs = []
            for device in ("cpu", "mps"):
                x = torch.tensor([base], dtype=dtype, device=device)
                source = torch.tensor([src], dtype=dtype, device=device)
                index = torch.tensor([0], device=device)
                result = torch.index_reduce(
                    x,
                    0,
                    index,
                    source,
                    reduce=reduce,
                    include_self=include_self,
                )
                outputs.append(result.cpu().tolist())

            print(
                dtype,
                reduce,
                base,
                src,
                include_self,
                "CPU:", outputs[0],
                "MPS:", outputs[1],
            )
```

Expected output:

The CPU and MPS results should both contain NaN in every case.

Actual output:

```text
float16 amax nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amax 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amax 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [-inf]
float16 amin nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amin 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amin 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [inf]

float32 amax nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amax 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amax 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [-inf]
float32 amin nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amin 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amin 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [inf]

bfloat16 amax nan 1.0 True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amax 1.0 nan True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amax 1.0 nan False CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin nan 1.0 True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin 1.0 nan True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin 1.0 nan False CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
```

### Preliminary investigation

The culprit is `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/Indexing.metal:IndexReduceOp`. The templates `amin` and `amax` uses Metal built-ins `min` and `max` instead of PyTorch's c10 metal operations (i.e. `c10::metal::min` and `c10::metal::max`). The native Metal kernels do not support NaN propagation in these cases. Using the `c10::metal` versions allow NaN to be propagated correctly. 

The apparent cause is `IndexReduceOp` in `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/Indexing.metal`:

```metal
return min(a, b); // return c10::metal::min(a, b);
return max(a, b); // return c10::metal::max(a, b);
```

Should be a simple fix - I can get it.

### Agent details

This initial analysis, reproduction matrix, and proposed fix were prepared with Codex. I've updated the issue description to make it more intuitive.

### Describe the bug

On MPS, `torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy` accepts a wider range of inputs than CPU. See examples below. This can silently produce misleading results e.g. a NaN input can produce a finite loss; an input outside [0, 1] can produce a negative loss. On CPU/CUDA backends, the inputs are validated.

We expect MPS to match CPU for these cases. 

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


values = (float("nan"), float("inf"), float("-inf"), -0.1, 1.1)

for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.float32, torch.bfloat16):
    for value in values:
        for target in (0.0, 1.0):
            outputs = []
            for device in ("cpu", "mps"):
                x = torch.tensor([value], device=device, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
                y = torch.tensor([target], device=device, dtype=dtype)
                try:
                    loss = F.binary_cross_entropy(x, y)
                    loss.backward()
                    if device == "mps":
                        torch.mps.synchronize()
                    outputs.append((float(loss.detach().cpu()), float(x.grad.cpu())))
                except Exception as error:
                    outputs.append((type(error).__name__, str(error).splitlines()[0]))
            if outputs[0] != outputs[1]:
                print(dtype, value, target)
                print("  CPU", outputs[0])
                print("  MPS", outputs[1])
```

### Describe the bug

On MPS, fused Adam with `amsgrad=True` can erase an existing NaN in the `max_exp_avg_sq` optimizer state. Recall that the intuition of `max_exp_avg_sq` optimizer state is to get a monotone non-decreasing denominator for the second moment of the gradients of a parameter, so that future gradient steps do not increase due to a shrinking uncorrected second moment estimator.

For CPU Adam and non-fused MPS Adam, NaNs are preserved. Fused MPS Adam replaces the NaN with a finite value in `max_exp_avg_sq`. This can silently hide invalid optimizer state, specifically states restored from a checkpoint. Note: if a gradient update is NaN, this NaN will propagate via the other optimizer states such as the first order moment estimator, which still leads to the parameter being NaN (correct result, because the bug is shadowed).

The same behaviour can be observed with AdamW and with `torch.float16`, `torch.float32`, and `torch.bfloat16`.

```python
import torch

def run(fused):
    parameter = torch.ones(2, device="mps", requires_grad=True)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
        [parameter], lr=0.1, amsgrad=True, fused=fused, foreach=False
    )

    parameter.grad = torch.ones_like(parameter)
    optimizer.step()

    state = optimizer.state[parameter]
    state["max_exp_avg_sq"][0] = float("nan")

    parameter.grad = torch.ones_like(parameter)
    optimizer.step()
    torch.mps.synchronize()

    return parameter.detach().cpu(), state["max_exp_avg_sq"].cpu()

print(torch.__version__)
print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available())

for fused in (False, True):
    parameter, max_exp_avg_sq = run(fused)
    print(f"fused={fused}")
    print("  parameter:", parameter.tolist())
    print("  max_exp_avg_sq:", max_exp_avg_sq.tolist())
```

Output:

```text
2.16.0a0+git8cd072a
MPS available: True
fused=False
  parameter: [nan, 0.800000011920929]
  max_exp_avg_sq: [nan, 0.0019990000873804092]
fused=True
  parameter: [0.7999988198280334, 0.7999988198280334]
  max_exp_avg_sq: [0.0019989742431789637, 0.0019989742431789637]
```

### Preliminary investigation

The AMSGrad update in `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/FusedOptimizerOps.metal` uses native Metal `max`:

```metal
max_exp_avg_sq = max(max_exp_avg_sq, exp_avg_sq);
```

As mentioned in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201148, native Metal `max` does not propagate an existing NaN in its first operand. Similarly for bfloat16. Instead, we should just use `c10::metal::max` in `c10/metal/utils.h`, which explicitly propagates NaNs, i.e.:

```metal
max_exp_avg_sq =
    c10::metal::max(max_exp_avg_sq, exp_avg_sq);
```

{"repository": "pytorch/pytorch", "task_candidate_id": 21899, "repository_id": 236, "issue_number": 201155, "github_issue_id": 5879567752, "html_url": "https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201155", "created_at": "2026-10-16T06:36:36+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "[MPS] Fused Adam/AdamW with AMSGrad erases NaN in `max_exp_avg_sq`", "body_text": "### Describe the bug

On MPS, fused Adam with `amsgrad=True` can erase an existing NaN in the `max_exp_avg_sq` optimizer state. Recall that the intuition of `max_exp_avg_sq` optimizer state is to get a monotone non-decreasing denominator for the second moment of the gradients of a parameter, so that future gradient steps do not increase due to a shrinking uncorrected second moment estimator.

For CPU Adam and non-fused MPS Adam, NaNs are preserved. Fused MPS Adam replaces the NaN with a finite value in `max_exp_avg_sq`. This can silently hide invalid optimizer state, specifically states restored from a checkpoint. Note: if a gradient update is NaN, this NaN will propagate via the other optimizer states such as the first order moment estimator, which still leads to the parameter being NaN (correct result, because the bug is shadowed).

The same behaviour can be observed with AdamW and with `torch.float16`, `torch.float32`, and `torch.bfloat16`.

```python
import torch

def run(fused):
    parameter = torch.ones(2, device="mps", requires_grad=True)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(
        [parameter], lr=0.1, amsgrad=True, fused=fused, foreach=False
    )

    parameter.grad = torch.ones_like(parameter)
    optimizer.step()

    state = optimizer.state[parameter]
    state["max_exp_avg_sq"][0] = float("nan")

    parameter.grad = torch.ones_like(parameter)
    optimizer.step()
    torch.mps.synchronize()

    return parameter.detach().cpu(), state["max_exp_avg_sq"].cpu()

print(torch.__version__)
print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available())

for fused in (False, True):
    parameter, max_exp_avg_sq = run(fused)
    print(f"fused={fused}")
    print("  parameter:", parameter.tolist())
    print("  max_exp_avg_sq:", max_exp_avg_sq.tolist())
```

Output:

```text
2.16.0a0+git8cd072a
MPS available: True
fused=False
  parameter: [nan, 0.800000011920929]
  max_exp_avg_sq: [nan, 0.0019990000873804092]
fused=True
  parameter: [0.7999988198280334, 0.7999988198280334]
  max_exp_avg_sq: [0.0019989742431789637, 0.0019989742431789637]
```

### Preliminary investigation

The AMSGrad update in `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/FusedOptimizerOps.metal` uses native Metal `max`:

```metal
max_exp_avg_sq = max(max_exp_avg_sq, exp_avg_sq);
```

As mentioned in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201148, native Metal `max` does not propagate an existing NaN in its first operand. Similarly for bfloat16. Instead, we should just use `c10::metal::max` in `c10/metal/utils.h`, which explicitly propagates NaNs, i.e.:

```metal
max_exp_avg_sq =
    c10::metal::max(max_exp_avg_sq, exp_avg_sq);
```

##### Cause and reproduction

Pattern: an eager SAC context (`checkpoint(fn, ..., use_reentrant=False, context_fn=...)` with `create_selective_checkpoint_contexts`) around an already `torch.compile`d `fn`. SAC traced by Dynamo inside the compiled region is not affected.

`_CachingTorchDispatchMode` ignores compile internals, so at runtime it sees the ops the Inductor wrapper dispatches (fallback, extern and custom ops such as SDPA or `view_as_complex`) and caches their outputs, which alias Inductor buffers. Inductor reuses those buffers after their last use in the graph. The write comes from a generated kernel, not through the dispatcher, so `_version` does not change and the "has been mutated" check does not fire. Ordinary recomputation-based AC does not use this operator-result cache.

This CPU test isolates cache corruption, not the training gradient spike. Requires only PyTorch; save as `repro.py` and run `python repro.py`. No backward pass is needed. It uses `memory_planning=True`; the default Inductor config also reproduces with `activation_memory_budget=0.37` (an in-place kernel overwrites the cached buffer; `test_checkpoint_gradients` in #201974).

```python
import torch
from torch._inductor import config
from torch.utils.checkpoint import create_selective_checkpoint_contexts


def fn(x, weight):
    z = torch.view_as_complex(x.sin())
    y = torch.view_as_real(z).reshape(64, 128)
    return y.cos() @ weight


torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(64, 64, 2)
weight = torch.randn(128, 128)
op = torch.ops.aten.view_as_complex.default
expected_saved = torch.view_as_complex(x.sin())
expected_output = fn(x, weight)
with config.patch(memory_planning=True, memory_pool="combined"):
    compiled = torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)
    forward, replay = create_selective_checkpoint_contexts([op])
    with forward:
        actual = compiled(x, weight)
    torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected_output)
    torch.testing.assert_close(forward.storage[op][0].val, expected_saved)
    with replay:
        repeated = compiled(x, weight)
    torch.testing.assert_close(repeated, expected_output)
print("PASS: cached value and replay match eager")
```

Forward matches eager, but all 4096 cached elements differ (the second `assert_close` fails). Expected: cache and replay both match eager.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`torch._functorch.benchmark_utils` treats `devices=["cuda"]` as the sync path and always records `ProfilerActivity.CUDA`.

On a renamed PrivateUse1 backend this follows the CUDA sentinel instead of the current accelerator, and the profiler activity does not match that device. `cpu:0` is also not treated as CPU, and a benchmark call rebinds the module-level `synchronize` used by later calls.

Trying to solve the issue I found out that `fcntl` module doesn't exist in Windows. Using information from this source https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45228395/error-no-module-named-fcntl I was able to replace it successfully with `portalocker` (https://github.com/wolph/portalocker). I had to modify 2 files: `...\site-packages\torch\_vendor\quack\cache\jit.py` and `...\site-packages\torch\_vendor\quack\cache\async_compile.py`.

Patches:
```
--- original\jit.py
+++ modified\jit.py
@@ -19,1 +19,1 @@
-import fcntl
+import portalocker
@@ -106,1 +106,1 @@
-        lock_type = fcntl.LOCK_EX if self.exclusive else fcntl.LOCK_SH
+        lock_type = portalocker.LOCK_EX if self.exclusive else portalocker.LOCK_SH
@@ -111,1 +111,1 @@
-                fcntl.flock(self._fd, lock_type | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
+                portalocker.lock(self._fd, lock_type | portalocker.LOCK_NB)
@@ -121,1 +121,1 @@
-            fcntl.flock(self._fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
+            portalocker.unlock(self._fd)
```

```
--- original\async_compile.py
+++ modified\async_compile.py
@@ -43,1 +43,1 @@
-import fcntl
+import portalocker
@@ -101,2 +101,2 @@
-            fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_SH | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
-            fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
+            portalocker.lock(fd, portalocker.LOCK_SH | portalocker.LOCK_NB)
+            portalocker.unlock(fd)
```
I am not a programmer by any stretch of imagination and I don't suggest that my "hack" is "the solution" but for my ComfyUI purposes it works (for now, I didn't make extensive testing).

As far I can figure out this is the PR that introduced this: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/186284

Trying to solve the issue I found out that `fcntl` module doesn't exist in Windows. Using information from this source https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45228395/error-no-module-named-fcntl I was able to replace it successfully with `portalocker` (https://github.com/wolph/portalocker). I had to modify 2 files: `...\site-packages\torch\_vendor\quack\cache\jit.py` and `...\site-packages\torch\_vendor\quack\cache\async_compile.py`.

Patches:
```
--- original\jit.py
+++ modified\jit.py
@@ -19,1 +19,1 @@
-import fcntl
+import portalocker
@@ -106,1 +106,1 @@
-        lock_type = fcntl.LOCK_EX if self.exclusive else fcntl.LOCK_SH
+        lock_type = portalocker.LOCK_EX if self.exclusive else portalocker.LOCK_SH
@@ -111,1 +111,1 @@
-                fcntl.flock(self._fd, lock_type | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
+                portalocker.lock(self._fd, lock_type | portalocker.LOCK_NB)
@@ -121,1 +121,1 @@
-            fcntl.flock(self._fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
+            portalocker.unlock(self._fd)
```

```
--- original\async_compile.py
+++ modified\async_compile.py
@@ -43,1 +43,1 @@
-import fcntl
+import portalocker
@@ -101,2 +101,2 @@
-            fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_SH | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
-            fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
+            portalocker.lock(fd, portalocker.LOCK_SH | portalocker.LOCK_NB)
+            portalocker.unlock(fd)
```
I am not a programmer by any stretch of imagination and I don't suggest that my "hack" is "the solution" but for my ComfyUI purposes it works (for now, I didn't make extensive testing).

As far I can figure out this is the PR that introduced this: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/186284
