### 🐛 Describe the bug

I ran into this while running LeRobot policies (SmolVLA, ACT) as ExecuTorch CUDA programs, which are compiled with AOTInductor, on a Jetson AGX Thor: the same Triton kernels were 15-30% slower there than under torch.compile. Giving those kernels the same shared-memory preference that Inductor's static launcher uses brought them back to torch.compile speed, so I'd expect AOTInductor's `loadKernel` to do the same. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the measurements were run on my machine and reviewed by me, and I have a patch with a test ready.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> The `loadKernel` that AOTInductor and the C++ wrapper embed (`CUDADeviceOpOverrides.kernel_driver()` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cuda/device_op_overrides.py`) sets only `CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_DYNAMIC_SHARED_SIZE_BYTES`. Inductor's static CUDA launcher, which `torch.compile` uses by default, also calls `cuFuncSetCacheConfig(func, CU_FUNC_CACHE_PREFER_SHARED)` for every kernel that uses more than 48 KB of shared memory (`torch/csrc/inductor/static_launcher/cuda.cpp`), and Triton's own launcher also prefers shared memory to L1 for those kernels. Without the preference, the driver may pick a shared-memory carveout that fits fewer of such a kernel's blocks per SM, so the same Triton kernel can run slower in an AOTInductor package than under `torch.compile`.
>
> On a Jetson AGX Thor, a module of four bf16 GEMMs (M x N x K of 1024x2048x2048, 2048x4096x4096, 4096x4096x4096 and 968x3072x768) was compiled with max-autotune and the 64x128x64 three-stage config of the reproducer below, so every variant runs the same kernels (73,744 bytes of shared memory each). Median time per call over 21 trials of 50 calls (the first three variants interleaved, the device-wide setting timed last):
>
> | Variant | ms per call |
> |---|---|
> | AOTInductor | 5.143 |
> | AOTInductor with the fix below | 3.359 |
> | `torch.compile` | 3.353 |
> | AOTInductor after `cudaDeviceSetCacheConfig(cudaFuncCachePreferShared)` | 3.359 |
>
> With the configs autotuning picks on its own (196,624 bytes, one block per SM whatever the carveout), all four take 2.33 to 2.37 ms. ExecuTorch's CUDA backend compiles its programs with AOTInductor, and there, on Thor, Triton kernels above 48 KB ran 15-30% slower than under `torch.compile`. Setting the preference device-wide in ExecuTorch's runtime took a SmolVLA action chunk from 33.1 to 30.6 ms and an ACT chunk from 2.75 to 2.56 ms. Nsight Compute could not confirm the blocks per SM, because it needs GPU counter permission on this board.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:aoti-kernel-prefer-shared](https://github.com/edmundshieh/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:aoti-kernel-prefer-shared): `loadKernel` makes the same call for kernels above 48 KB, which hipifies to the `hipFuncSetCacheConfig` call the static launcher makes on ROCm. It will be sent as a PR once this issue is triaged.

Reproducer:

```python
import re
import zipfile

import torch
import torch._inductor.utils

# Inductor autotunes GEMM templates only on GPUs with at least 68 SMs; this line
# is needed on smaller ones (the run below is on a 20-SM Jetson Thor).
torch._inductor.utils.is_big_gpu = lambda *args: True


class MM(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, a, b):
        return a @ b


args = (
    torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16),
    torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16),
)
options = {
    "max_autotune": True,
    "max_autotune_gemm_backends": "TRITON",
    # Inductor's 64x128x64 three-stage mm config, which needs 73,744 bytes of shared memory.
    "test_configs.autotune_choice_desc_regex": "BLOCK_K=64, BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=128, .*num_stages=3, num_warps=4$",
}
path = torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(
    torch.export.export(MM(), args), package_path="mm.pt2", inductor_configs=options
)
with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:
    src = next(z.read(n).decode() for n in z.namelist() if n.endswith(".cpp") and "/model/" in n)
for name, smem in re.findall(r'loadKernel\([^;]*?"(\w+)",\s*(\d+)', src):
    print(f"loadKernel({name}, sharedMemBytes={smem})")
print("cuFuncSetCacheConfig in the wrapper:", "cuFuncSetCacheConfig" in src)
```

Output:

```
loadKernel(triton_tem_fused_mm_0, sharedMemBytes=73744)
cuFuncSetCacheConfig in the wrapper: False
```

### Error logs

No error: the generated `loadKernel` sets no shared-memory preference for a kernel that needs 73,744 bytes of shared memory, while `torch.compile` launches the same kernel with `CU_FUNC_CACHE_PREFER_SHARED`.

I ran into this while running LeRobot policies (SmolVLA, ACT) as ExecuTorch CUDA programs, which are compiled with AOTInductor, on a Jetson AGX Thor: the same Triton kernels were 15-30% slower there than under torch.compile. Giving those kernels the same shared-memory preference that Inductor's static launcher uses brought them back to torch.compile speed, so I'd expect AOTInductor's `loadKernel` to do the same. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the measurements were run on my machine and reviewed by me, and I have a patch with a test ready.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> The `loadKernel` that AOTInductor and the C++ wrapper embed (`CUDADeviceOpOverrides.kernel_driver()` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cuda/device_op_overrides.py`) sets only `CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_DYNAMIC_SHARED_SIZE_BYTES`. Inductor's static CUDA launcher, which `torch.compile` uses by default, also calls `cuFuncSetCacheConfig(func, CU_FUNC_CACHE_PREFER_SHARED)` for every kernel that uses more than 48 KB of shared memory (`torch/csrc/inductor/static_launcher/cuda.cpp`), and Triton's own launcher also prefers shared memory to L1 for those kernels. Without the preference, the driver may pick a shared-memory carveout that fits fewer of such a kernel's blocks per SM, so the same Triton kernel can run slower in an AOTInductor package than under `torch.compile`.
>
> On a Jetson AGX Thor, a module of four bf16 GEMMs (M x N x K of 1024x2048x2048, 2048x4096x4096, 4096x4096x4096 and 968x3072x768) was compiled with max-autotune and the 64x128x64 three-stage config of the reproducer below, so every variant runs the same kernels (73,744 bytes of shared memory each). Median time per call over 21 trials of 50 calls (the first three variants interleaved, the device-wide setting timed last):
>
> | Variant | ms per call |
> |---|---|
> | AOTInductor | 5.143 |
> | AOTInductor with the fix below | 3.359 |
> | `torch.compile` | 3.353 |
> | AOTInductor after `cudaDeviceSetCacheConfig(cudaFuncCachePreferShared)` | 3.359 |
>
> With the configs autotuning picks on its own (196,624 bytes, one block per SM whatever the carveout), all four take 2.33 to 2.37 ms. ExecuTorch's CUDA backend compiles its programs with AOTInductor, and there, on Thor, Triton kernels above 48 KB ran 15-30% slower than under `torch.compile`. Setting the preference device-wide in ExecuTorch's runtime took a SmolVLA action chunk from 33.1 to 30.6 ms and an ACT chunk from 2.75 to 2.56 ms. Nsight Compute could not confirm the blocks per SM, because it needs GPU counter permission on this board.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:aoti-kernel-prefer-shared](https://github.com/edmundshieh/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:aoti-kernel-prefer-shared): `loadKernel` makes the same call for kernels above 48 KB, which hipifies to the `hipFuncSetCacheConfig` call the static launcher makes on ROCm. It will be sent as a PR once this issue is triaged.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

I noticed this while autotuning bf16 GEMMs on a Jetson AGX Thor: Inductor's Blackwell warp-specialized GEMM template never appeared among the candidates. Thor has the same tcgen05 tensor cores as B200, but CUDA 13 renumbered it from sm_101 to sm_110, so the arch check now leaves it out; I'd expect it to be treated like sm_100 here, as flex attention already does. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the tests were run on my machine and reviewed by me, and I have a patch with a test ready.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> `is_datacenter_blackwell_arch()` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cuda/cuda_env.py` holds only for `100 <= arch < 110`. Jetson Thor was sm_101 until CUDA 13 renumbered it sm_110, so it falls outside that range, although it has the same tcgen05 tensor cores and TMA as sm_100; consumer Blackwell (sm_120) has no tcgen05. So on Thor, max-autotune with `triton.enable_persistent_tma_matmul` never offers the warp-specialized TMA GEMM template (`blackwell_ws_persistent_tma`), and the opt-in CuTeDSL grouped GEMM template, which checks the same function, is off too. `has_datacenter_blackwell_tma_device()` in `torch/utils/_triton.py` has the same range (`(10, 0) <= capability < (11, 0)`), so every test in `test/inductor/test_max_autotune_blackwell.py` is skipped on Thor.
>
> With both checks widened to capability major 10 or 11, as flex attention's FLASH backend already does, the template works on Thor. With the option on, ExecuTorch's CUDA backend, which compiles with AOTInductor and max-autotune, autotuned 31 candidates instead of 21 for a 4096x2048x2048 bf16 matmul on Thor, and the template won: 0.382 ms against 0.414 ms for the best other one. Large-M bf16 GEMMs ran 20-44% faster with it in isolation. The Blackwell template tests, run on Thor against the nightly below with `is_big_gpu` forced on (Thor has 20 SMs), gave 79 passed and no failures: the TMA store and load fusion, autoWS and exhaustive-config classes, and 37 `TestMaxAutotuneBlackwell` cases, not the full parametrized sweep.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:inductor-blackwell-template-sm110](https://github.com/edmundshieh/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:inductor-blackwell-template-sm110): both checks accept sm_110, and sm_120 stays out. It will be sent as a PR once this issue is triaged.

Reproducer:

```python
import torch
from torch._inductor.codegen.cuda.cuda_env import is_datacenter_blackwell_arch
from torch.utils._triton import (
    has_datacenter_blackwell_tma_device,
    has_triton_tensor_descriptor_host_tma,
    has_triton_tma_device,
)

print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(), torch.cuda.get_device_capability())
print("has_triton_tma_device():", has_triton_tma_device())
print("has_triton_tensor_descriptor_host_tma():", has_triton_tensor_descriptor_host_tma())
print("is_datacenter_blackwell_arch():", is_datacenter_blackwell_arch())
print("has_datacenter_blackwell_tma_device():", has_datacenter_blackwell_tma_device())
```

Output:

```

has_triton_tma_device(): True
has_triton_tensor_descriptor_host_tma(): True
is_datacenter_blackwell_arch(): False
has_datacenter_blackwell_tma_device(): False
```

### Error logs

No error: on Thor, `is_datacenter_blackwell_arch()` returns False, so the Blackwell GEMM templates are never autotuned there, and their tests are skipped.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

I hit this writing the GeGLU MLP of a robot policy (pi0.5) as a `triton_op`. One Triton kernel computes the gate and up projections and writes the activation with TMA stores; a second reads it back with TMA loads for the down projection, both with 128x128 blocks. Exported through ExecuTorch's CUDA backend (AOTInductor) on a Jetson AGX Thor, the policy ran faster than it should have and its actions came out NaN; torch.compile gave NaN too, while eager was correct. Storing the activation with a different block shape works around it, but I'd expect Inductor to keep a kernel whose output a later kernel reads. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the reproducer and tests were run on my machine and reviewed by me, and I have a patch with a test ready.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> Inductor deduplicates host-side TMA descriptors: `TMADescriptor.create` in `torch/_inductor/ir.py` keeps one descriptor node per `(id(tensor), tma_meta)` in a class-level cache ("as TMA descriptors are immutable, we can dedup them by the input args"). A descriptor node reads its tensor when it is created, and the scheduler resolves that read against the mutations registered before the node. So when a user-defined Triton kernel A writes a tensor through a `TensorDescriptor` and a later kernel B reads the tensor through a descriptor with the same block shape, B gets A's descriptor node and depends on the tensor as it was before A, not on A's write. If nothing else reads what A wrote, as for an intermediate allocated inside a `triton_op`, A's output has no users and `Scheduler.dead_node_elimination` removes A. The generated code still builds A's descriptors but never launches A, so B reads uninitialized memory. torch.compile and AOTInductor both return wrong results; eager is right.
>
> In the reproducer below, a `triton_op` scales `x` by 2 into `h`, then `h` by 3 into `y`, with `[256]` blocks for both launches. The wrapper builds descriptors for `x`, `h` and `y` and launches only the second kernel, with the `h` descriptor built for the first. A different block shape for the write than for the read avoids the bug, because the two descriptors are then not deduplicated. The run below used torch 2.15.0.dev20261005 and Triton 3.9.0 on a Jetson AGX Thor; main has the same descriptor cache.
>
> A fix with a test is on [edmundshieh/pytorch:inductor-tma-descriptor-mutation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/compare/main...edmundshieh:pytorch:inductor-tma-descriptor-mutation): the cache moves to `GraphLowering`, and `mark_buffer_mutated` drops the descriptors of a mutated buffer and of its aliases, so a later reader creates its own descriptor, which depends on the write. With it, the reproducer prints `True` twice and the wrapper launches both kernels. It will be sent as a PR once this issue is triaged.

Reproducer:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from torch._inductor.utils import run_and_get_code
from torch.library import triton_op, wrap_triton
from triton.tools.tensor_descriptor import TensorDescriptor


@triton.jit
def scale_kernel(in_desc, out_desc, scale, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offset = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK
    out_desc.store([offset], in_desc.load([offset]) * scale)


def scale(x, out, s, block=256):
    wrap_triton(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), block),)](
        TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(x, [block]),
        TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(out, [block]),
        s,
        BLOCK=block,
    )


@triton_op("repro::scale_twice", mutates_args={})
def scale_twice(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    h = torch.empty_like(x)
    scale(x, h, 2.0)  # writes h through a [256] descriptor
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    scale(h, y, 3.0)  # reads h through a [256] descriptor
    return y


class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.ops.repro.scale_twice(x)


x = torch.randn(4096, device="cuda")
compiled, (code,) = run_and_get_code(torch.compile(Model()), x)
package = torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(torch.export.export(Model(), (x,)))
aoti = torch._inductor.aoti_load_package(package)(x)
eager = Model()(x)
print("torch.compile matches eager:", torch.allclose(compiled, eager))
print("AOTInductor matches eager:", torch.allclose(aoti, eager))
print("torch.compile wrapper code:")
for line in code.splitlines():
    if "TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(" in line or "scale_kernel_0.run(" in line:
        print("   ", line.strip())
```

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> Inductor deduplicates host-side TMA descriptors: `TMADescriptor.create` in `torch/_inductor/ir.py` keeps one descriptor node per `(id(tensor), tma_meta)` in a class-level cache ("as TMA descriptors are immutable, we can dedup them by the input args"). A descriptor node reads its tensor when it is created, and the scheduler resolves that read against the mutations registered before the node. So when a user-defined Triton kernel A writes a tensor through a `TensorDescriptor` and a later kernel B reads the tensor through a descriptor with the same block shape, B gets A's descriptor node and depends on the tensor as it was before A, not on A's write. If nothing else reads what A wrote, as for an intermediate allocated inside a `triton_op`, A's output has no users and `Scheduler.dead_node_elimination` removes A. The generated code still builds A's descriptors but never launches A, so B reads uninitialized memory. torch.compile and AOTInductor both return wrong results; eager is right.
>
> In the reproducer below, a `triton_op` scales `x` by 2 into `h`, then `h` by 3 into `y`, with `[256]` blocks for both launches. The wrapper builds descriptors for `x`, `h` and `y` and launches only the second kernel, with the `h` descriptor built for the first. A different block shape for the write than for the read avoids the bug, because the two descriptors are then not deduplicated. The run below used torch 2.15.0.dev20261005 and Triton 3.9.0 on a Jetson AGX Thor; main has the same descriptor cache.
>

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I ran into this while tuning the Triton kernels of a `triton_op` (the GeGLU MLP of the pi0.5 robot policy) with torch.compile on a Jetson AGX Thor. After I changed a kernel's launch config, the next run still executed the old kernels, so a timing I took for the new config actually came from the previous one. Turning off the AOTAutograd cache with `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0` fixed it. I'd expect any edit to a `triton_op`'s code to miss the cache, as editing a kernel the op launches directly already does. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the reproducer was run on my machine and reviewed by me. I don't have a fix ready and would like a maintainer's view on the options at the end of the analysis.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> A `torch.library.triton_op` is traced into the compiled graph: AOTAutograd replaces the op with the `triton_kernel_wrapper_*` calls its body makes, so the compiled code bakes in the body and its kernels. The AOTAutograd cache (`torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/autograd_cache.py`) keys the Dynamo graph, where the op is a call to `torch.ops.<namespace>.<name>`. `check_node_safe` accepts any `OpOverload`, and the op's implementation enters the key only through `triton_kernel_source_codes`: the sources of the kernels that `torch._library.triton.get_inner_triton_kernels` finds when it scans the op's source at registration. Edits outside what the scan finds leave the key unchanged, and a warm cache returns the compile from before the edit:
>
> - the op's own code, e.g. a scalar or launch parameter it passes to a kernel, its grid, or the torch ops it calls;
> - kernels the scan does not reach, e.g. one launched through a helper that receives `wrap_triton` as an argument, or through a call on a module attribute such as `kernels.launch(...)`. When all of an op's launches go through such helpers, the key includes no kernel source at all.
>
> On a hit, AOTAutograd loads the compiled code that its entry bundles or references by FX graph cache key, so Inductor's FX graph cache, whose key covers the traced kernels, never sees the edited op. A `torch.library.custom_op` is not affected, since its implementation runs at run time instead of being traced into the graph.
>
> The reproducer compiles a `triton_op` in two fresh processes that share a cache directory, and edits the op's source between them, for three kinds of edit. After the first two, the second process gets an AOTAutograd cache hit and returns the result from before the edit. Editing a kernel that the op launches itself changes the key, and the second process recompiles. With `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0`, which keeps Inductor's FX graph cache, all three return the edited result. The runs below used torch 2.15.0.dev20261005 and Triton 3.9.0 on a Jetson AGX Thor; main has the same key computation and source scan.
>
> Possible fixes: also hash the source of the op and of the functions the scan already walks, or bypass the AOTAutograd cache for graphs that call a `triton_op`.

Reproducer:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

OP = """
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from torch.library import triton_op, wrap_triton


@triton.jit
def scale_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, scale, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x * scale * KERNEL_FACTOR, mask=mask)


def launch(x, out, scale, wrap):
    wrap(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, scale, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)


@triton_op("repro::scale", mutates_args={})
def scale(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    LAUNCH
    return out
"""
DIRECT = "wrap_triton(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, BODY_SCALE, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)"
HELPER = "launch(x, out, BODY_SCALE, wrap_triton)"

RUN = """
import torch
import repro_op
from torch._dynamo.utils import counters

y = torch.compile(lambda x: torch.ops.repro.scale(x))(torch.ones(8, device="cuda"))
print(y[0].item(), counters["aot_autograd"]["autograd_cache_hit"])
"""

# (description, launch, (body scale, kernel factor) before and after the edit)
CASES = [
    ("edit the scalar the op passes to its kernel", DIRECT, [("2.0", "1.0"), ("3.0", "1.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched through a helper", HELPER, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched by the op itself", DIRECT, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
]

for description, launch, versions in CASES:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        env = dict(
            os.environ,
            PYTHONPATH=tmp,
            PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1",
            TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=os.path.join(tmp, "inductor"),
        )
        results = []
        for body_scale, kernel_factor in versions:
            source = OP.replace("LAUNCH", launch).replace("BODY_SCALE", body_scale)
            with open(os.path.join(tmp, "repro_op.py"), "w") as f:
                f.write(source.replace("KERNEL_FACTOR", kernel_factor))
            out = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, "-c", RUN], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
            ).stdout.split()
            expected = float(body_scale) * float(kernel_factor)
            results.append(f"expected {expected}, got {float(out[0])} (AOTAutograd cache hits: {out[1]})")
        print(f"{description}:\n  before: {results[0]}\n  after:  {results[1]}")
```

  before: expected 2.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)
  after:  expected 3.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 1)
edit the kernel, launched through a helper:
  before: expected 2.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)
  after:  expected 3.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 1)
edit the kernel, launched by the op itself:
  before: expected 2.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)
  after:  expected 3.0, got 3.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)

I ran into this while tuning the Triton kernels of a `triton_op` (the GeGLU MLP of the pi0.5 robot policy) with torch.compile on a Jetson AGX Thor. After I changed a kernel's launch config, the next run still executed the old kernels, so a timing I took for the new config actually came from the previous one. Turning off the AOTAutograd cache with `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0` fixed it. I'd expect any edit to a `triton_op`'s code to miss the cache, as editing a kernel the op launches directly already does. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the reproducer was run on my machine and reviewed by me. I don't have a fix ready and would like a maintainer's view on the options at the end of the analysis.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> A `torch.library.triton_op` is traced into the compiled graph: AOTAutograd replaces the op with the `triton_kernel_wrapper_*` calls its body makes, so the compiled code bakes in the body and its kernels. The AOTAutograd cache (`torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/autograd_cache.py`) keys the Dynamo graph, where the op is a call to `torch.ops.<namespace>.<name>`. `check_node_safe` accepts any `OpOverload`, and the op's implementation enters the key only through `triton_kernel_source_codes`: the sources of the kernels that `torch._library.triton.get_inner_triton_kernels` finds when it scans the op's source at registration. Edits outside what the scan finds leave the key unchanged, and a warm cache returns the compile from before the edit:
>
> - the op's own code, e.g. a scalar or launch parameter it passes to a kernel, its grid, or the torch ops it calls;
> - kernels the scan does not reach, e.g. one launched through a helper that receives `wrap_triton` as an argument, or through a call on a module attribute such as `kernels.launch(...)`. When all of an op's launches go through such helpers, the key includes no kernel source at all.
>
> On a hit, AOTAutograd loads the compiled code that its entry bundles or references by FX graph cache key, so Inductor's FX graph cache, whose key covers the traced kernels, never sees the edited op. A `torch.library.custom_op` is not affected, since its implementation runs at run time instead of being traced into the graph.
>
> The reproducer compiles a `triton_op` in two fresh processes that share a cache directory, and edits the op's source between them, for three kinds of edit. After the first two, the second process gets an AOTAutograd cache hit and returns the result from before the edit. Editing a kernel that the op launches itself changes the key, and the second process recompiles. With `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0`, which keeps Inductor's FX graph cache, all three return the edited result. The runs below used torch 2.15.0.dev20261005 and Triton 3.9.0 on a Jetson AGX Thor; main has the same key computation and source scan.
>
> Possible fixes: also hash the source of the op and of the functions the scan already walks, or bypass the AOTAutograd cache for graphs that call a `triton_op`.

Reproducer:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

OP = """
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from torch.library import triton_op, wrap_triton


@triton.jit
def scale_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, scale, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x * scale * KERNEL_FACTOR, mask=mask)


def launch(x, out, scale, wrap):
    wrap(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, scale, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)


@triton_op("repro::scale", mutates_args={})
def scale(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    LAUNCH
    return out
"""
DIRECT = "wrap_triton(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, BODY_SCALE, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)"
HELPER = "launch(x, out, BODY_SCALE, wrap_triton)"

RUN = """
import torch
import repro_op
from torch._dynamo.utils import counters

y = torch.compile(lambda x: torch.ops.repro.scale(x))(torch.ones(8, device="cuda"))
print(y[0].item(), counters["aot_autograd"]["autograd_cache_hit"])
"""

# (description, launch, (body scale, kernel factor) before and after the edit)
CASES = [
    ("edit the scalar the op passes to its kernel", DIRECT, [("2.0", "1.0"), ("3.0", "1.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched through a helper", HELPER, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched by the op itself", DIRECT, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
]

for description, launch, versions in CASES:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        env = dict(
            os.environ,
            PYTHONPATH=tmp,
            PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1",
            TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=os.path.join(tmp, "inductor"),
        )
        results = []
        for body_scale, kernel_factor in versions:
            source = OP.replace("LAUNCH", launch).replace("BODY_SCALE", body_scale)
            with open(os.path.join(tmp, "repro_op.py"), "w") as f:
                f.write(source.replace("KERNEL_FACTOR", kernel_factor))
            out = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, "-c", RUN], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
            ).stdout.split()
            expected = float(body_scale) * float(kernel_factor)
            results.append(f"expected {expected}, got {float(out[0])} (AOTAutograd cache hits: {out[1]})")
        print(f"{description}:\n  before: {results[0]}\n  after:  {results[1]}")

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

While speeding up tensordict for robotics RL libraries, I timed the minibatch gathers in their PPO updates on CPU across torch versions. rsl_rl, for example, gathers each minibatch with `values[batch_idx]`, `advantages[batch_idx]`, `returns[batch_idx]` and `old_actions_log_prob[batch_idx]`, which are all (N, 1) tensors.

Since 2.14.0, `x[idx]` with a 1-D int64 index takes twice as long on 1-D and (N, 1) tensors as it did in 2.13.0. Wider rows and `index_select` did not change. Chasing that down led me to the single-index loop that #190658 added to the CPU indexing kernel: a source build of main without that loop is back to the 2.13 speed. I expected 2.14 to keep the 2.13 speed.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.benchmark import Timer

torch.set_num_threads(1)
idx = torch.randint(0, 98_304, (24_576,))
print(torch.__version__)
for shape in [(98_304,), (98_304, 1), (98_304, 108)]:
    x = torch.randn(shape)
    t_index = Timer("x[idx]", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    t_select = Timer("x.index_select(0, idx)", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    print(f"{str(shape):13s} x[idx] {t_index.median * 1e6:7.1f} us   index_select {t_select.median * 1e6:7.1f} us")
```

```
2.13.0+cpu
(98304,)      x[idx]    33.7 us   index_select     8.5 us
(98304, 1)    x[idx]    33.8 us   index_select    45.6 us
(98304, 108)  x[idx]  1349.3 us   index_select   384.9 us

2.16.0.dev20261016+cpu
(98304,)      x[idx]    77.1 us   index_select     8.4 us
(98304, 1)    x[idx]    77.3 us   index_select    44.9 us
(98304, 108)  x[idx]  1380.4 us   index_select   366.9 us
```

I had an agent investigate further; below is the AI-assisted analysis.

### AI-assisted analysis

An AI coding agent (Claude, in the Pi harness) ran the measurements below at my request, bisected them over releases and nightlies, and read the history of the CPU indexing kernel. I reviewed its findings before filing.

> `x[idx]` for 24,576 int64 indices into 98,304 float32 rows on an otherwise idle AMD EPYC 9R45 (AWS m8a.4xlarge), one version at a time, pinned to one core. Each time is the minimum of five `blocked_autorange` medians:
>
> | torch | `(98304,)` | `(98304, 1)` |
> |---|---:|---:|
> | 2.4.1 | 32.3 us | 32.4 us |
> | 2.8.0 | 34.9 us | 34.8 us |
> | 2.9.1 | 35.0 us | 35.1 us |
> | 2.10.0 | 34.8 us | 34.8 us |
> | 2.11.0 | 34.7 us | 35.0 us |
> | 2.12.1 | 34.8 us | 35.0 us |
> | 2.13.0 | 34.1 us | 34.0 us |
> | 2.14.1 | 68.4 us | 68.6 us |
> | 2.15.0 | 77.0 us | 77.3 us |
> | 2.16.0.dev20261016 | 77.0 us | 77.2 us |
>
> - With 14 threads, the 1-D case went from 8.5 us (2.4.1) and 9.3 us (2.8.0) to 12.9 us (2.14.1) and 14.1-14.3 us (2.15.0 and the nightly).
> - The other kernel builds show the same step. With `ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2`, 2.13.0 takes 35.6 us and 2.14.1 takes 68.5 us; with `ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=default`, 34.8 us and 76.2 us.
> - The toolchain did not change: the `.comment` section of `libtorch_cpu.so` reads GCC 13.3.1 in every wheel from 2.13.0 to the nightly, and none of them has BOLT sections.
> - Fixed costs did not move: 384 indices into a (24576, 108) tensor take 13.3-14.2 us in every release from 2.4.1 to the nightly.
> - Between v2.13.0 and v2.14.0, the only change to [`aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h#L18-L102) is 6893e6967aca (#190658, "Add single-index-tensor fast path to cpu_index_kernel loop", 2026-07-23). `IndexKernel.cpp` changed only in its dtype lists (`kBComplex32`).
> - That commit adds `Indexer::get_1` and a third loop in `cpu_index_kernel`, used when there is one index tensor and the index stride inside the loop is not zero. For a 1-D or (N, 1) source, the inner loop of the TensorIterator runs over the indices, so every element goes through the new loop. For wider rows, the inner loop runs along one row with index stride 0 and takes the `is_constant_index` branch, which the commit did not touch. This matches the shapes that slowed down and the ones that did not.
> - A CPU-only source build of main (f9990bc) with GCC 13.4 reproduces it: `(98304,)` takes 82.1 us. Removing only the `else if (indexer.num_indexers == 1)` branch, so that these gathers go back to the generic `indexer.get(i)` loop, brings it down to 35.5 us, the 2.13.0 speed. With 14 threads, it goes from 14.9 to 9.5 us.
> - #190658 does not report a benchmark, so we do not know which case the new loop was meant to speed up. We did not look at the generated code.
> - The smaller step from 69 to 77 us is not a separate regression. The daily nightlies from 2026-09-26 to 2026-10-04 alternate between the two (69.9, 77.1, 77.0, 77.0, 69.2, 69.4, 76.8 and 77.0 us) while the indexing sources stay the same, which points to code layout in each build.

title: [CPU] `x[idx]` on 1-D tensors is 2x slower since 2.14.0

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

While speeding up tensordict for RL libraries such as rsl_rl and LeanRL, I found that pulling a minibatch out of the rollout buffer, `td[idx]`, was the most expensive tensordict call in their PPO updates on CPU. It indexes every tensor in the buffer with the same 1-D int64 index.

Chasing that down took me to `aten::index` itself. With a 1-D integer index along dim 0 of a contiguous tensor, `x[idx]` is 3-7x slower than `x.index_select(0, idx)`, which returns the same tensor. The gap is there in every release I tried, from 2.4.1 to the latest nightly.

I think this should be fixed because `x[idx]` is how most code writes a row gather, and the CUDA kernel already has a fast path for this case (#151917). I expected the two to run at about the same speed. I have a prototype of a fix along the lines of the CUDA one, with numbers in the analysis below, and I'm happy to turn it into a PR.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.benchmark import Timer

torch.set_num_threads(1)
print(torch.__version__)
for n_rows, row, n_idx, dtype in [
    (24_576, 108, 384, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 8, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 48, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 108, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 512, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 108, 24_576, torch.bfloat16),
]:
    x = torch.randn(n_rows, row).to(dtype)
    idx = torch.randint(0, n_rows, (n_idx,))
    assert torch.equal(x[idx], x.index_select(0, idx))
    t_index = Timer("x[idx]", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    t_select = Timer("x.index_select(0, idx)", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    print(
        f"{n_idx:6d} of ({n_rows}, {row:3d}) {str(dtype)[6:]:8s}  "
        f"x[idx] {t_index.median * 1e6:7.1f} us   index_select {t_select.median * 1e6:7.1f} us   "
        f"{t_index.median / t_select.median:4.1f}x"
    )
```

```

   384 of (24576, 108) float32   x[idx]    13.6 us   index_select     4.3 us    3.2x
 24576 of (98304,   8) float32   x[idx]   193.7 us   index_select    60.5 us    3.2x
 24576 of (98304,  48) float32   x[idx]   618.7 us   index_select   109.4 us    5.7x
 24576 of (98304, 108) float32   x[idx]  1636.2 us   index_select   380.1 us    4.3x
 24576 of (98304, 512) float32   x[idx] 16569.6 us   index_select 10729.4 us    1.5x

I had an agent investigate further; below is the AI-assisted analysis.

### AI-assisted analysis

An AI coding agent (Claude, in the Pi harness) ran the measurements below at my request and read the CPU indexing code on `main` (f9990bc). I reviewed its findings before filing.

> All times are from an otherwise idle AMD EPYC 9R45 (AWS m8a.4xlarge), one torch version at a time, pinned to one core unless noted.
>
> The repro above on ten releases (2.4.1, 2.8.0, 2.9.1, 2.10.0, 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0, 2.14.1, 2.15.0 and 2.16.0.dev20261016), one thread. Each cell is the range over the ten:
>
> | Case | `x[idx]` | `index_select` | Ratio (median) |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | 384 of (24576, 108) float32 | 13.3-14.2 us | 3.8-4.1 us | 3.2-3.6x (3.4x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 8) float32 | 168-212 us | 53-67 us | 2.6-3.9x (3.2x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 48) float32 | 589-664 us | 104-118 us | 5.3-6.1x (5.5x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) float32 | 1188-1646 us | 332-393 us | 3.4-4.8x (3.8x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 512) float32 | 16.0-17.3 ms | 9.4-10.4 ms | 1.6-1.8x (1.7x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) bfloat16 | 1022-1254 us | 143-160 us | 6.7-8.3x (7.1x) |
>
> With 14 threads (cores 2-15), on 2.16.0.dev20261016: 24,576 rows of 108 float32 take 85.0 us with `x[idx]` against 23.9 us with `index_select` (3.6x); rows of 48 float32, 39.5 against 10.0 us (3.9x); bfloat16 rows of 108, 75.0 against 12.5 us (6.0x). For 384 indices, both take about 6.5 us.
>
> **Why `x[idx]` is slower**
>
> - `x[idx]` runs the CPU `index_kernel` ([cpu/IndexKernel.cpp L24-L41](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp#L24-L41)), which calls `cpu_index_kernel` ([cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h L18-L102](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h#L18-L102)) with a functor that copies one element.
> - For `x` of shape (N, D) and `idx` of shape (M,), the TensorIterator has shape (D, M) in iterator order, with byte strides out `(4, 4D)`, src `(4, 0)`, idx `(0, 8)`. The two dims cannot be coalesced, so the loop body runs once per output row with `n = D`. Each call builds an `Indexer`, takes the `is_constant_index` branch, bounds-checks and wraps the index, then makes D scalar copies at strides known only at run time.
> - `index_select_out_cpu_` ([TensorAdvancedIndexing.cpp L1621-L1885](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorAdvancedIndexing.cpp#L1621-L1885)) checks once that the slices are contiguous and then makes one bounds check and one `memcpy` per row, in `at::parallel_for` blocks of `GRAIN_SIZE / slice_size` rows (from #30598, 2020).
> - `index` also does more work before the loop: `make_info`, `expandTensors`, `expand_outplace`, `restride_src`, `reshape_indexer` and a 3-operand TensorIterator build. The prototype below shows that the copy loop still dominates, even for 384 indices.
> - The CUDA `index` kernel already sends this layout to a gather kernel: `fast_gather_kernel_eligible` ([cuda/IndexKernelUtils.h L13-L36](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/IndexKernelUtils.h#L13-L36)), called from `gpu_index_kernel` ([cuda/IndexKernel.cu L76-L90](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/IndexKernel.cu#L76-L90)), added in #151917. It requires `iter.ndim() == 2`, index strides `{0, index_elsize}`, `strides(0)[0] == strides(1)[0] == elsize` and `strides(1)[1] == 0`, which matches the CPU iterator's layout above. The CPU kernel has no such check.
> - #116555 (open) reports the same gap for `dim=-1`. There, @mingfeima wrote that `index` "treat[s] it in a pointwise way. If your benchmark `dim = 0`, you will probably find that `index_select` outperforms `index`."
> - The element-wise copy dates from the TensorIterator rewrite in #13420 (2018). The later changes to these files (#69607, #102601, #190658, #199435, #199509, plus dtype and COW changes) did not change how a row is copied.
>
> **Possible fix**
>
> Port the CUDA check to the CPU `index_kernel`. When it holds, loop over the M output rows in `at::parallel_for`; for each row, load the index, wrap a negative value, bounds-check it, and copy the `D * elsize` bytes of the source row with one `memcpy`. Single-element gathers, from 1-D and (N, 1) sources, can get a direct loop the same way. The op stays `aten::index`, so autograd, negative indices and dtype coverage do not change. Rerouting `x[idx]` to `index_select` would change the error messages and reject negative indices, and the two ops have different backward formulas.
>
> A prototype of this change, about 80 lines in `cpu/IndexKernel.cpp` (below), was measured on a CPU-only source build of main (f9990bc, GCC 13.4). The "before" build is main with the `get_1` loop of #190658 removed, because that loop slows down 1-D gathers on its own (#201246). One thread:
>
> | Case | `x[idx]` before | `x[idx]` with the prototype | `index_select` |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | 384 of (24576, 108) float32 | 13.3 us | 4.8 us | 4.0 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 8) float32 | 173 us | 76 us | 54 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 48) float32 | 615 us | 132 us | 115 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) float32 | 1381 us | 454 us | 392 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 512) float32 | 16.9 ms | 11.0 ms | 10.4 ms |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) bfloat16 | 1105 us | 192 us | 159 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304,) float32 | 35.5 us | 15.3 us | 8.8 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 1) float32 | 35.4 us | 14.8 us | 47.4 us |
>
> With 14 threads, 24,576 rows of 108 float32 go from 84.2 to 26.4 us (`index_select`: 25.2 us), bfloat16 rows from 81.8 to 15.1 us (13.2 us), 65,536 of (1000000, 48) float32 from 184.5 to 39.1 us (36.8 us), and the 1-D gather from 9.5 to 6.8 us (9.0 us).
>
> The prototype passes `test/test_indexing.py` (184 passed), the CPU tests in `test/test_torch.py` and `test/test_ops.py` that match `index`, `gather`, `take` or `getitem` (43 and 508 passed, 67 xfailed), and a byte-for-byte comparison of `x[idx]` with a Python-loop reference (672 cases). The reference cases cover 16 dtypes; strided, sliced, flipped and expanded sources; multi-dimensional and strided index tensors; `out=`; error messages; autograd; and 8 threads. bool tensors keep the old loop, because `c10::load` normalizes bool bytes and `memcpy` would not.
>
> **torch.compile**
>
> Inductor lowers `aten.index` to its own loop and decomposes `index_select` into `x[idx]`, so both forms compile to the same code and neither calls the eager kernel. On 2.16.0.dev20261016 with one thread, the compiled gather of 24,576 rows of 108 float32 takes about 320 us in either form, against 1424 us for eager `x[idx]` and 402 us for eager `index_select`. For 384 indices, the compiled call takes about 9 us, against 13.6 us and 3.9 us eager.
>
> **One-element rows**
>
> For (N, 1) tensors the order is reversed: `index_select` takes about 45 us in every release, against 34 us for `x[idx]` in 2.13.0. In 2.14.0 and later, `x[idx]` on 1-D and (N, 1) tensors takes 68-77 us; that regression is #201246.

<details>
<summary>Prototype patch (against f9990bc)</summary>

```diff
--- a/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp
+++ b/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp
@@ -2,6 +2,8 @@
 #include <ATen/native/IndexKernel.h>
 
 #include <cmath>
+#include <cstring>
+#include <type_traits>
 #include <iostream>
 
 #include <ATen/Context.h>
@@ -21,11 +23,91 @@
 
 using namespace vec;
 
+// Fast paths for a gather with one int64 index tensor, as in the CUDA kernel's
+// fast_gather_kernel_eligible: copy each indexed slice whole when it is contiguous in
+// both src and dst (iterator shape (slice, n)), or copy one element per index when the
+// slice is a single element (iterator shape (n,)). Returns false for any other layout.
+template <typename scalar_t>
+bool cpu_index_gather_fast(TensorIteratorBase& iter, IntArrayRef index_size, IntArrayRef index_stride) {
+  if (index_size.size() != 1 || iter.ntensors() != 3 || iter.numel() == 0 ||
+      iter.element_size(2) != static_cast<int64_t>(sizeof(int64_t))) {
+    return false;
+  }
+  constexpr int64_t elsize = sizeof(scalar_t);
+  const int64_t size = index_size[0];
+  const int64_t src_index_stride = index_stride[0];
+  char* const out = static_cast<char*>(iter.data_ptr(0));
+  char* const src = static_cast<char*>(iter.data_ptr(1));
+  const char* const idx = static_cast<const char*>(iter.data_ptr(2));
+  auto load_index = [size, idx](int64_t i, int64_t idx_stride) {
+    int64_t value = *reinterpret_cast<const int64_t*>(idx + i * idx_stride);
+    TORCH_CHECK_INDEX(value >= -size && value < size,
+                      "index ", value, " is out of bounds for dimension 0 with size ", size);
+    return value < 0 ? value + size : value;
+  };
+  if (iter.ndim() == 2) {
+    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<scalar_t, bool>) {
+      return false;  // c10::load normalizes bool bytes; memcpy would not
+    } else {
+      const auto out_s = iter.strides(0);
+      const auto src_s = iter.strides(1);
+      const auto idx_s = iter.strides(2);
+      const int64_t slice = iter.shape()[0];
+      const int64_t slice_bytes = slice * elsize;
+      if (out_s[0] != elsize || src_s[0] != elsize || src_s[1] != 0 || idx_s[0] != 0 ||
+          out_s[1] < slice_bytes) {
+        return false;
+      }
+      at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[1], std::max<int64_t>(1, at::internal::GRAIN_SIZE / slice),
+                       [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+        for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+          const int64_t value = load_index(i, idx_s[1]);
+          std::memcpy(out + i * out_s[1], src + value * src_index_stride, slice_bytes);
+        }
+      });
+      return true;
+    }
+  }
+  if (iter.ndim() == 1 && iter.strides(1)[0] == 0) {
+    const int64_t out_s = iter.strides(0)[0];
+    const int64_t idx_s = iter.strides(2)[0];
+    if (out_s == elsize && idx_s == static_cast<int64_t>(sizeof(int64_t))) {
+      // contiguous output and index: a plain typed loop the compiler can unroll
+      scalar_t* const out_data = reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(out);
+      const int64_t* const idx_data = reinterpret_cast<const int64_t*>(idx);
+      at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[0], 3000, [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+        for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+          int64_t value = idx_data[i];
+          TORCH_CHECK_INDEX(value >= -size && value < size,
+                            "index ", value, " is out of bounds for dimension 0 with size ", size);
+          if (value < 0) {
+            value += size;
+          }
+          out_data[i] = c10::load(reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(src + value * src_index_stride));
+        }
+      });
+      return true;
+    }
+    at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[0], 3000, [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+      for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+        const int64_t value = load_index(i, idx_s);
+        *reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(out + i * out_s) =
+            c10::load(reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(src + value * src_index_stride));
+      }
+    });
+    return true;
+  }
+  return false;
+}
+
 void index_kernel(TensorIteratorBase& iter, IntArrayRef index_size, IntArrayRef index_stride) {
   AT_DISPATCH_V2(
     iter.dtype(),
     "index_cpu",
     AT_WRAP([&] {
+      if (cpu_index_gather_fast<scalar_t>(iter, index_size, index_stride)) {
+        return;
+      }
       cpu_index_kernel<scalar_t>(iter, index_size, index_stride, [](char* dst, char* src, int64_t offset) {
         *(scalar_t*)dst = c10::load((scalar_t*)(src + offset));
       });
```

While speeding up tensordict for RL libraries such as rsl_rl and LeanRL, I found that pulling a minibatch out of the rollout buffer, `td[idx]`, was the most expensive tensordict call in their PPO updates on CPU. It indexes every tensor in the buffer with the same 1-D int64 index.

Chasing that down took me to `aten::index` itself. With a 1-D integer index along dim 0 of a contiguous tensor, `x[idx]` is 3-7x slower than `x.index_select(0, idx)`, which returns the same tensor. The gap is there in every release I tried, from 2.4.1 to the latest nightly.

I think this should be fixed because `x[idx]` is how most code writes a row gather, and the CUDA kernel already has a fast path for this case (#151917). I expected the two to run at about the same speed. I have a prototype of a fix along the lines of the CUDA one, with numbers in the analysis below, and I'm happy to turn it into a PR.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.benchmark import Timer

torch.set_num_threads(1)
print(torch.__version__)
for n_rows, row, n_idx, dtype in [
    (24_576, 108, 384, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 8, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 48, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 108, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 512, 24_576, torch.float32),
    (98_304, 108, 24_576, torch.bfloat16),
]:
    x = torch.randn(n_rows, row).to(dtype)
    idx = torch.randint(0, n_rows, (n_idx,))
    assert torch.equal(x[idx], x.index_select(0, idx))
    t_index = Timer("x[idx]", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    t_select = Timer("x.index_select(0, idx)", globals={"x": x, "idx": idx}).blocked_autorange(min_run_time=1)
    print(
        f"{n_idx:6d} of ({n_rows}, {row:3d}) {str(dtype)[6:]:8s}  "
        f"x[idx] {t_index.median * 1e6:7.1f} us   index_select {t_select.median * 1e6:7.1f} us   "
        f"{t_index.median / t_select.median:4.1f}x"
    )

### AI-assisted analysis

An AI coding agent (Claude, in the Pi harness) ran the measurements below at my request and read the CPU indexing code on `main` (f9990bc). I reviewed its findings before filing.

> All times are from an otherwise idle AMD EPYC 9R45 (AWS m8a.4xlarge), one torch version at a time, pinned to one core unless noted.
>
> The repro above on ten releases (2.4.1, 2.8.0, 2.9.1, 2.10.0, 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0, 2.14.1, 2.15.0 and 2.16.0.dev20261016), one thread. Each cell is the range over the ten:
>
> | Case | `x[idx]` | `index_select` | Ratio (median) |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | 384 of (24576, 108) float32 | 13.3-14.2 us | 3.8-4.1 us | 3.2-3.6x (3.4x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 8) float32 | 168-212 us | 53-67 us | 2.6-3.9x (3.2x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 48) float32 | 589-664 us | 104-118 us | 5.3-6.1x (5.5x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) float32 | 1188-1646 us | 332-393 us | 3.4-4.8x (3.8x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 512) float32 | 16.0-17.3 ms | 9.4-10.4 ms | 1.6-1.8x (1.7x) |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) bfloat16 | 1022-1254 us | 143-160 us | 6.7-8.3x (7.1x) |
>
> With 14 threads (cores 2-15), on 2.16.0.dev20261016: 24,576 rows of 108 float32 take 85.0 us with `x[idx]` against 23.9 us with `index_select` (3.6x); rows of 48 float32, 39.5 against 10.0 us (3.9x); bfloat16 rows of 108, 75.0 against 12.5 us (6.0x). For 384 indices, both take about 6.5 us.
>
> **Why `x[idx]` is slower**
>
> - `x[idx]` runs the CPU `index_kernel` ([cpu/IndexKernel.cpp L24-L41](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp#L24-L41)), which calls `cpu_index_kernel` ([cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h L18-L102](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernelUtils.h#L18-L102)) with a functor that copies one element.
> - For `x` of shape (N, D) and `idx` of shape (M,), the TensorIterator has shape (D, M) in iterator order, with byte strides out `(4, 4D)`, src `(4, 0)`, idx `(0, 8)`. The two dims cannot be coalesced, so the loop body runs once per output row with `n = D`. Each call builds an `Indexer`, takes the `is_constant_index` branch, bounds-checks and wraps the index, then makes D scalar copies at strides known only at run time.
> - `index_select_out_cpu_` ([TensorAdvancedIndexing.cpp L1621-L1885](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorAdvancedIndexing.cpp#L1621-L1885)) checks once that the slices are contiguous and then makes one bounds check and one `memcpy` per row, in `at::parallel_for` blocks of `GRAIN_SIZE / slice_size` rows (from #30598, 2020).
> - `index` also does more work before the loop: `make_info`, `expandTensors`, `expand_outplace`, `restride_src`, `reshape_indexer` and a 3-operand TensorIterator build. The prototype below shows that the copy loop still dominates, even for 384 indices.
> - The CUDA `index` kernel already sends this layout to a gather kernel: `fast_gather_kernel_eligible` ([cuda/IndexKernelUtils.h L13-L36](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/IndexKernelUtils.h#L13-L36)), called from `gpu_index_kernel` ([cuda/IndexKernel.cu L76-L90](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f9990bc15141f4490b4d70944517bf44455327dd/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/IndexKernel.cu#L76-L90)), added in #151917. It requires `iter.ndim() == 2`, index strides `{0, index_elsize}`, `strides(0)[0] == strides(1)[0] == elsize` and `strides(1)[1] == 0`, which matches the CPU iterator's layout above. The CPU kernel has no such check.
> - #116555 (open) reports the same gap for `dim=-1`. There, @mingfeima wrote that `index` "treat[s] it in a pointwise way. If your benchmark `dim = 0`, you will probably find that `index_select` outperforms `index`."
> - The element-wise copy dates from the TensorIterator rewrite in #13420 (2018). The later changes to these files (#69607, #102601, #190658, #199435, #199509, plus dtype and COW changes) did not change how a row is copied.
>
> **Possible fix**
>
> Port the CUDA check to the CPU `index_kernel`. When it holds, loop over the M output rows in `at::parallel_for`; for each row, load the index, wrap a negative value, bounds-check it, and copy the `D * elsize` bytes of the source row with one `memcpy`. Single-element gathers, from 1-D and (N, 1) sources, can get a direct loop the same way. The op stays `aten::index`, so autograd, negative indices and dtype coverage do not change. Rerouting `x[idx]` to `index_select` would change the error messages and reject negative indices, and the two ops have different backward formulas.
>
> A prototype of this change, about 80 lines in `cpu/IndexKernel.cpp` (below), was measured on a CPU-only source build of main (f9990bc, GCC 13.4). The "before" build is main with the `get_1` loop of #190658 removed, because that loop slows down 1-D gathers on its own (#201246). One thread:
>
> | Case | `x[idx]` before | `x[idx]` with the prototype | `index_select` |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | 384 of (24576, 108) float32 | 13.3 us | 4.8 us | 4.0 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 8) float32 | 173 us | 76 us | 54 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 48) float32 | 615 us | 132 us | 115 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) float32 | 1381 us | 454 us | 392 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 512) float32 | 16.9 ms | 11.0 ms | 10.4 ms |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 108) bfloat16 | 1105 us | 192 us | 159 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304,) float32 | 35.5 us | 15.3 us | 8.8 us |
> | 24,576 of (98304, 1) float32 | 35.4 us | 14.8 us | 47.4 us |
>
> With 14 threads, 24,576 rows of 108 float32 go from 84.2 to 26.4 us (`index_select`: 25.2 us), bfloat16 rows from 81.8 to 15.1 us (13.2 us), 65,536 of (1000000, 48) float32 from 184.5 to 39.1 us (36.8 us), and the 1-D gather from 9.5 to 6.8 us (9.0 us).
>
> The prototype passes `test/test_indexing.py` (184 passed), the CPU tests in `test/test_torch.py` and `test/test_ops.py` that match `index`, `gather`, `take` or `getitem` (43 and 508 passed, 67 xfailed), and a byte-for-byte comparison of `x[idx]` with a Python-loop reference (672 cases). The reference cases cover 16 dtypes; strided, sliced, flipped and expanded sources; multi-dimensional and strided index tensors; `out=`; error messages; autograd; and 8 threads. bool tensors keep the old loop, because `c10::load` normalizes bool bytes and `memcpy` would not.
>
> **torch.compile**
>
> Inductor lowers `aten.index` to its own loop and decomposes `index_select` into `x[idx]`, so both forms compile to the same code and neither calls the eager kernel. On 2.16.0.dev20261016 with one thread, the compiled gather of 24,576 rows of 108 float32 takes about 320 us in either form, against 1424 us for eager `x[idx]` and 402 us for eager `index_select`. For 384 indices, the compiled call takes about 9 us, against 13.6 us and 3.9 us eager.
>
> **One-element rows**
>
> For (N, 1) tensors the order is reversed: `index_select` takes about 45 us in every release, against 34 us for `x[idx]` in 2.13.0. In 2.14.0 and later, `x[idx]` on 1-D and (N, 1) tensors takes 68-77 us; that regression is #201246.

<summary>Prototype patch (against f9990bc)</summary>

```diff
--- a/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp
+++ b/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/IndexKernel.cpp
@@ -2,6 +2,8 @@
 #include <ATen/native/IndexKernel.h>
 
 #include <cmath>
+#include <cstring>
+#include <type_traits>
 #include <iostream>
 
 #include <ATen/Context.h>
@@ -21,11 +23,91 @@
 
 using namespace vec;
 
+// Fast paths for a gather with one int64 index tensor, as in the CUDA kernel's
+// fast_gather_kernel_eligible: copy each indexed slice whole when it is contiguous in
+// both src and dst (iterator shape (slice, n)), or copy one element per index when the
+// slice is a single element (iterator shape (n,)). Returns false for any other layout.
+template <typename scalar_t>
+bool cpu_index_gather_fast(TensorIteratorBase& iter, IntArrayRef index_size, IntArrayRef index_stride) {
+  if (index_size.size() != 1 || iter.ntensors() != 3 || iter.numel() == 0 ||
+      iter.element_size(2) != static_cast<int64_t>(sizeof(int64_t))) {
+    return false;
+  }
+  constexpr int64_t elsize = sizeof(scalar_t);
+  const int64_t size = index_size[0];
+  const int64_t src_index_stride = index_stride[0];
+  char* const out = static_cast<char*>(iter.data_ptr(0));
+  char* const src = static_cast<char*>(iter.data_ptr(1));
+  const char* const idx = static_cast<const char*>(iter.data_ptr(2));
+  auto load_index = [size, idx](int64_t i, int64_t idx_stride) {
+    int64_t value = *reinterpret_cast<const int64_t*>(idx + i * idx_stride);
+    TORCH_CHECK_INDEX(value >= -size && value < size,
+                      "index ", value, " is out of bounds for dimension 0 with size ", size);
+    return value < 0 ? value + size : value;
+  };
+  if (iter.ndim() == 2) {
+    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<scalar_t, bool>) {
+      return false;  // c10::load normalizes bool bytes; memcpy would not
+    } else {
+      const auto out_s = iter.strides(0);
+      const auto src_s = iter.strides(1);
+      const auto idx_s = iter.strides(2);
+      const int64_t slice = iter.shape()[0];
+      const int64_t slice_bytes = slice * elsize;
+      if (out_s[0] != elsize || src_s[0] != elsize || src_s[1] != 0 || idx_s[0] != 0 ||
+          out_s[1] < slice_bytes) {
+        return false;
+      }
+      at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[1], std::max<int64_t>(1, at::internal::GRAIN_SIZE / slice),
+                       [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+        for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+          const int64_t value = load_index(i, idx_s[1]);
+          std::memcpy(out + i * out_s[1], src + value * src_index_stride, slice_bytes);
+        }
+      });
+      return true;
+    }
+  }
+  if (iter.ndim() == 1 && iter.strides(1)[0] == 0) {
+    const int64_t out_s = iter.strides(0)[0];
+    const int64_t idx_s = iter.strides(2)[0];
+    if (out_s == elsize && idx_s == static_cast<int64_t>(sizeof(int64_t))) {
+      // contiguous output and index: a plain typed loop the compiler can unroll
+      scalar_t* const out_data = reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(out);
+      const int64_t* const idx_data = reinterpret_cast<const int64_t*>(idx);
+      at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[0], 3000, [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+        for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+          int64_t value = idx_data[i];
+          TORCH_CHECK_INDEX(value >= -size && value < size,
+                            "index ", value, " is out of bounds for dimension 0 with size ", size);
+          if (value < 0) {
+            value += size;
+          }
+          out_data[i] = c10::load(reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(src + value * src_index_stride));
+        }
+      });
+      return true;
+    }
+    at::parallel_for(0, iter.shape()[0], 3000, [&](int64_t begin, int64_t end) {
+      for (int64_t i = begin; i < end; i++) {
+        const int64_t value = load_index(i, idx_s);
+        *reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(out + i * out_s) =
+            c10::load(reinterpret_cast<scalar_t*>(src + value * src_index_stride));
+      }
+    });
+    return true;
+  }
+  return false;
+}
+
 void index_kernel(TensorIteratorBase& iter, IntArrayRef index_size, IntArrayRef index_stride) {
   AT_DISPATCH_V2(
     iter.dtype(),
     "index_cpu",
     AT_WRAP([&] {
+      if (cpu_index_gather_fast<scalar_t>(iter, index_size, index_stride)) {
+        return;
+      }
       cpu_index_kernel<scalar_t>(iter, index_size, index_stride, [](char* dst, char* src, int64_t offset) {
         *(scalar_t*)dst = c10::load((scalar_t*)(src + offset));
       });

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## 🐛 Bug
When exporting a trained model via Libtorch (C++ API), I hit two separate failures:
1. Export trained model to ONNX format failed.
2. Export trained model to AOT (torch.export / AOTInductor) format also failed.

The model is trained in Python PyTorch first, then loaded into Libtorch C++ for deployment. Both ONNX export and AOT export throw runtime exceptions and cannot generate valid model artifacts.

## To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Train a neural network model in Python PyTorch, save checkpoint.
2. Load the trained checkpoint into Libtorch C++ code.
3. Try to export the loaded model to ONNX using Libtorch ONNX export API → error.
4. Try to export the same loaded model to AOTInductor / AOT format via Libtorch → another error.

Minimal code snippet (C++ Libtorch):
```cpp
// Pseudocode
auto model = torch::jit::load("trained_model.pt");
std::vector<torch::jit::IValue> inputs;
inputs.push_back(torch::randn({1, 3, 224, 224}));

// 1. ONNX Export (failed)
torch::jit::export_to_onnx(model, "model.onnx", inputs);

// 2. AOT Export (failed)
// AOTInductor / AOT export API call here


ull error stack traces will be attached below after I capture the exact runtime messages.

## Expected behavior

Libtorch C++ API should successfully export the pre-trained loaded model to both ONNX and AOT format without exceptions, producing valid export files for inference deployment.

## Environment

- PyTorch / Libtorch version: [fill your version e.g. 2.5.1]
- OS: [e.g. Ubuntu 22.04 / Windows]
- Build: Prebuilt libtorch release / compiled from source
- C++ Compiler: [e.g. GCC 11 / MSVC 19]

## Additional context

My use case is pure C++ deployment pipeline: model training in Python, then model loading + export all inside Libtorch, no Python interpreter in export phase.
Currently both ONNX and AOT export paths in Libtorch are blocked for trained loaded models.

Please help investigate and fix these two bugs in Libtorch export APIs.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

While working on `torch.compile` support in TensorDict, I noticed that `td[:, a:]` recompiles every time `a` changes, even with `dynamic=True` (pytorch/tensordict#2889). Slicing a tensor the same way compiles once.

Chasing that down, it looks like the cause is in Dynamo. If a slice has a dynamic bound, a simple check on it, like `s is None`, `s is Ellipsis`, or `if not index` on a tuple that holds it, makes Dynamo guard on the bound's current value. So every new size recompiles, even though none of these checks depends on the bound.

I think this is worth fixing because a lot of `__getitem__` code starts with checks like these, and nothing tells you that `dynamic=True` stopped working until you hit the recompile limit. I'd expect one graph for all sizes, as without the check:

```python
import torch
from torch._dynamo.utils import counters


def with_is_none(x, y):
    s = slice(y.shape[0], None)
    if s is None:
        return x
    return x[:, s]


def with_not(x, y):
    index = (slice(None), slice(y.shape[0], None))
    if not index:
        return x
    return x[index]


def without_check(x, y):
    return x[:, y.shape[0] :]


x = torch.randn(2, 32)
for fn in (with_is_none, with_not, without_check):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    counters.clear()
    compiled = torch.compile(fn, dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)
    for n in (5, 7, 9):
        compiled(x, torch.zeros(n))
    print(f"{fn.__name__:14s} graphs compiled for 3 sizes: {counters['stats']['unique_graphs']}")
```

Output, the same on 2.13.0, 2.14.1 and the 2.16.0.dev20261007 nightly:

```
with_is_none   graphs compiled for 3 sizes: 3
with_not       graphs compiled for 3 sizes: 3
without_check  graphs compiled for 3 sizes: 1
```

I had an agent investigate further; below is the AI-assisted analysis.

### Error logs

None. Nothing raises and the results are right; each new size just recompiles. `TORCH_LOGS=dynamic,recompiles` for `with_is_none`, called with sizes 5 and 7:

```
eval Eq(s17, 5) [guard added] if s is None:  # ./repro.py:7 in with_is_none (_dynamo/variables/tensor.py:2849 in evaluate_expr)
[__recompiles] Recompiling function with_is_none in ./repro.py:5
[__recompiles]     triggered by the following guard failure(s):
[__recompiles]     - 0/0: tensor 'y' size mismatch at index 0. expected 5, actual 7

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On CPU (MKL), `torch.add` accepts a CSR `out` whose `values()` is a non-overlapping stride-2 view, but writes the result as if it were contiguous. The second logical value is left unchanged.

```python
import torch

crow = torch.tensor([0, 1, 2], dtype=torch.int64)
cols = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int64)
lhs = torch.sparse_csr_tensor(crow.clone(), cols.clone(), torch.tensor([1., 2.]), size=(2, 2), check_invariants=True)
rhs = torch.sparse_csr_tensor(crow.clone(), cols.clone(), torch.tensor([10., 20.]), size=(2, 2), check_invariants=True)

backing = torch.tensor([-99., -88., -99., -77.])
out = torch.sparse_csr_tensor(crow.clone(), cols.clone(), backing[::2], size=(2, 2), check_invariants=True)

torch.add(lhs, rhs, out=out)
print(out.values().tolist())   # [11.0, -99.0], expected [11.0, 22.0]
print(backing.tolist())        # [11.0, 22.0, -99.0, -77.0]
```

The `out` tensor is valid (`check_invariants=True` passes). A contiguous CSR `out` returns `[11.0, 22.0]`. The result copy in `mkl_result_copy_` writes `nnz` scalars linearly regardless of the destination values stride, so either the stride should be honored or the layout rejected.

### Describe the bug

i've got a fix for this ready: https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/pytorch/commit/981ca2a691c

#### AI-generated reproducer

`Poisson` accepts a zero rate, but its KL divergence to itself and to a positive-rate Poisson distribution returns `NaN`. A zero-rate Poisson distribution is concentrated at zero, so the expected values in this example are `[0, 1, inf]`.

```python
import torch
from torch.distributions import Poisson, kl_divergence

p = Poisson(torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]))
q = Poisson(torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]))
print(torch.__version__)
print(kl_divergence(p, q))
```

Observed:

```text
2.16.0.dev20261016+cpu
tensor([nan, nan, inf])
```

|---|---|
| `tensor([nan, nan, inf])` | `tensor([0., 1., inf])` |

body_text:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under `torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16)`, `torch.compile` returns a wrong gradient
for `log_softmax(conv(x))` whenever any op follows the `log_softmax` inside the graph.

The repro compares two functions with identical backward by construction: `f2` only adds
a detached term (`q + (clamp_min(q, b) - q).detach()`). In eager their gradients agree
exactly. Compiled, they disagree, and the error grows with the magnitude of the logits.
A common offset on all logits changes nothing mathematically, since softmax is
shift-invariant.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(48, 48, 1).cuda()
h = torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda")
w = torch.softmax(2 * torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda"), dim=1)


def f1(t):
    return F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)


def f2(t):  # same values up to a detached term, same gradient
    q = F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)
    return q + (torch.clamp_min(q, -20.0) - q).detach()


def grad(f, compiled):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    fn = torch.compile(f) if compiled else f
    t = h.clone().requires_grad_()
    with torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16):
        out = fn(t)
    (-(w * out.float()).sum()).backward()
    return t.grad


for offset in (0.0, 100.0, 1000.0):  # common logit offset: softmax-invariant
    with torch.no_grad():
        conv.weight.normal_(0, 0.6)
        conv.bias.fill_(-offset)
    for compiled in (False, True):
        g1, g2 = grad(f1, compiled), grad(f2, compiled)
        cos = F.cosine_similarity(g1.flatten(), g2.flatten(), dim=0).item()
        print(f"offset {offset:6.0f} compiled={compiled!s:5}: "
              f"cos(grad f1, grad f2) = {cos:.4f}, |g2|/|g1| = {(g2.norm() / g1.norm()).item():.3f}")
```

Output:

```
offset      0 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset      0 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.9919, |g2|/|g1| = 1.018
offset   1000 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset   1000 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.6943, |g2|/|g1| = 2.295
```

### What the generated code does

- The **forward kernel** adds the conv bias in fp32 and computes `amax` and log-sum-exp
  from these unrounded fp32 logits. It stores the logits into the conv's **bf16** output
  buffer, and saves that buffer for the backward together with `amax` and the log-sum-exp.
- The **backward kernel** recomputes `log_softmax` as `bf16_logits - amax - lse`, i.e. it
  mixes rounded logits with statistics of the unrounded ones. `exp()` of that is not the

Under `torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16)`, `torch.compile` returns a wrong gradient
for `log_softmax(conv(x))` whenever any op follows the `log_softmax` inside the graph.

The repro compares two functions with identical backward by construction: `f2` only adds
a detached term (`q + (clamp_min(q, b) - q).detach()`). In eager their gradients agree
exactly. Compiled, they disagree, and the error grows with the magnitude of the logits.
A common offset on all logits changes nothing mathematically, since softmax is
shift-invariant.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(48, 48, 1).cuda()
h = torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda")
w = torch.softmax(2 * torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda"), dim=1)


def f1(t):
    return F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)


def f2(t):  # same values up to a detached term, same gradient
    q = F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)
    return q + (torch.clamp_min(q, -20.0) - q).detach()


def grad(f, compiled):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    fn = torch.compile(f) if compiled else f
    t = h.clone().requires_grad_()
    with torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16):
        out = fn(t)
    (-(w * out.float()).sum()).backward()
    return t.grad


for offset in (0.0, 100.0, 1000.0):  # common logit offset: softmax-invariant
    with torch.no_grad():
        conv.weight.normal_(0, 0.6)
        conv.bias.fill_(-offset)
    for compiled in (False, True):
        g1, g2 = grad(f1, compiled), grad(f2, compiled)
        cos = F.cosine_similarity(g1.flatten(), g2.flatten(), dim=0).item()
        print(f"offset {offset:6.0f} compiled={compiled!s:5}: "
              f"cos(grad f1, grad f2) = {cos:.4f}, |g2|/|g1| = {(g2.norm() / g1.norm()).item():.3f}")

body_text:
### Describe the bug

I tested the behavior when a CUDA SymmetricMemory rendezvous fails on a specific rank. By artificially injecting a peer-import or peer-map failure on Rank 0, Rank 1 returned after approximately 301 seconds, with the imported resources remaining unreleased. Although local tensor health checks passed on both ranks, the subsequent rendezvous operation within the same group failed during the metadata exchange phase. These results come from injected-fault testing, with one run per case, rather than the reproduction of a failure under a real-world workload.

#### AI-assisted technical report

AI assistance was used for the diagnostic and this report. Two processes shared one RTX 4090, using a Gloo group, the Store-exchange/POSIX-FD route, overlapping-device allowance and multicast disabled. The shim temporarily intercepts process-local DriverAPI calls; only rank 0's first peer import or map is failed.

H/R/M below denotes imported-handle references, address reservations and mappings remaining when the first call returned:

| Case | Rank 0 | Rank 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Success | Success; fresh same-group second rendezvous and peer-data checks also passed on both ranks |
| Import failure | Error in 0.012 s; H/R/M 0/0/0; received FD still open | `RuntimeError("Wait timeout")` after 301 s; H/R/M 1/1/1 |
| Map failure | Error in 0.012 s; H/R/M 1/1/0; received FD still open | Same 301 s wait and H/R/M 1/1/1 |

The normal resources have committed owners; they are not leaks. Fault-case leftovers were measured while processes remained alive, before teardown. FD evidence is an open descriptor with matching identity at first return, not a complete close-call trace. The map case's rank-0 reservation leak is the already-known #201091 problem, not a new finding.

With injection disabled and fresh allocations, both fault-case retries failed in about 6 s: rank 0 waited for `CUDASymmetricMemory/1/1`, while rank 1 waited for `CUDASymmetricMemory/2/0`. Neither reached a new peer import. Both ranks observed metadata keys `0/0`, `0/1`, `1/0`, `2/1` present, with `1/1` and `2/0` absent. This corroborates exchange-sequence divergence; counters were not directly instrumented. Retry was a diagnostic, not an assertion that same-group recovery is currently supported.

The Store timeout was configured and read back as 5 s. The 301 s peer wait is consistent with the PrefixStore barrier's inherited timeout; that is a separate c10d concern, not the proposed fix here.

#### Source explanation

On the audited source, rank 0 throws inside the [peer-import loop](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1039) before reaching the [Store barrier](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1078). Rank 1 waits there. Peer [AllocationRef owners are constructed only afterward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1121), leaving its imports and mappings without an owner when the barrier throws. Rank 0 also skips the barrier's exchange sequence, consistent with the divergent metadata keys observed on retry.

The diagnostic and sanitized evidence are linked below.

https://gist.github.com/jackLei0901/cf4c1ff43d39504291f084b4fc391975

#### Scope and limits

The tested library is a local build on reported pin `215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8`, containing an earlier draft of #201091's local `alloc()` change. Its peer-rendezvous code, StoreExchange and Store code match `74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533`; this is not a complete current-main build or the shared-helper revision in #201284.

No fix arm, two-physical-GPU run, NCCL process-group (`use_pg`) path, multicast, Fabric, ROCm, fatal CUDA error or process-loss case was tested. vLLM fallback relevance is source-based, not a serving reproduction.

#### Reporter conclusion and scope question

kapilsh, do you think it would be appropriate to use the existing `MulticastSetup` coordinated-outcome pattern to handle the subsequent processing for the peer setup phase? My goal is for the participating ranks to reach a consensus on success or failure, and—in the event of failure—to release the peer handles, mappings, and received file descriptors (FDs) they have acquired.

Should the agreed-upon behavior be limited strictly to "prompt coordinated failure handling and resource cleanup" (with the caller responsible for recreating the group or terminating the program), or should it also support "subsequent rendezvous within the same group"? This decision will determine the scope of the exchange sequence logic and the regression testing strategy. I haven't implemented the fix for coordinated failure handling yet; unless you need to support the "retry within the same group" feature, I plan to exclude it from the current implementation scope.

### Versions

PyTorch: 2.16.0a0+git2158569; reported pin: 215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8.
CUDA build: 13.0; driver: 595.71.05; OS: Linux; GPU: one RTX 4090 shared by two processes.
Backend: CUDA SymmetricMemory; allocator: native, expandable segments disabled.
